### Epic 127 — Compiler/diagnostic findings from corpus-regen harness tuning (2026-07-13)

**Why:** while tuning the Gate-3 corpus regeneration harness (6-program sample round against tkc 2.8.0), four defects surfaced via compile+runtime probes. All reproduce on minimal programs; none are tracked elsewhere (checked Epics 110–126). Corpus impact: each is a silent-wrong-behaviour or crash class that would poison generated training data if workers hit them. **Update 2026-09-18:** Epic 131.2 decides a **fix-now** set (recommended 127.2, 127.6–127.10 — their workarounds would otherwise become the "canonical" forms in the pattern catalogue); those fixes stay as 127.x stories and **block 131.11 (syntax card v2)**.

| ID | Story | Status | Priority | Notes |
|----|-------|--------|----------|-------|
| 127.1 | UFCS method call silently drops extra arguments | open | P1 | `let c=a.concat("A";"B");` on `a="xx"` compiles clean and yields `"xxA"` — the receiver becomes arg1, `"A"` arg2, and `"B"` is DISCARDED with no diagnostic. Method-style dispatch must arity-check against the resolved signature (receiver counts as first param) and reject surplus args (expected E4-class error). Repro: `m=t;i=io:std.io;f=main():i64{let a="xx";let c=a.concat("A";"B");io.println(c);<0};` → prints `xxA`. **131.2 disposition (2026-09-18, `docs/architecture/127-disposition-131.md`, tkc 2.8.0 built from `386cf3d`):** reproduced (also module-style `s.concat(a;"A";"B")`); **workaround-is-canonical** — bundle the fix with 127.5 (`types.c:1125` has no arity check for non-user callees; size M). |
| 127.2 | Bare `.push(v)` statement crashes at runtime | not-reproducible (2026-09-18) → close via 127.3 | P1 | `let a=mut.@(1;2);a.push(9);` compiles, then the binary exits 1 before any output (also on `mut.@()`). Reassigned form `a=a.push(9);` works (len 3). Discarding a value-semantic result should be at worst a no-op — never a crash. Related: 114.3 established value semantics as intended; this is the crash case, not the discard case. **131.2 disposition (2026-09-18, `docs/architecture/127-disposition-131.md`, tkc 2.8.0 built from `386cf3d`):** **NOT reproducible on 2.8.0** — bare `.push(v)`/`.append(v)`/`.set(i;v)` statements are a silent no-op (exit 0) in every variant probed, not a crash. Close as not-reproducible once 127.3 lands (the silent no-op is the real hazard). |
| 127.3 | Diagnostic: warn on discarded value-semantic method result | in_progress (via 131.9) | P1 | Corpus-quality lever for 127.2's whole class: statement-position `arr.set(i;v);` / `arr.push(v);` / `m2.set(k;v);` compile silently and mutate nothing. A W-level "result of value-semantic method discarded — did you mean `x=x.set(...)`?" (with fix field) would catch the single most common LLM-generated logic bug observed in harness tuning (v1 sample round: bubble sort compiled + ran + returned the input unsorted). **131.2 disposition (2026-09-18, `docs/architecture/127-disposition-131.md`, tkc 2.8.0 built from `386cf3d`):** **promoted to fix-now** — shipped as the `discarded-value-result` lint **error** in 131.9 (bare `arr.set/push/append`, `m.set` in statement position). |

Until fixed, idiom rule 7 (combinators over loops) is only safe for `map`/`filter`; the regen syntax card steers workers to `lp` + `append` for reductions. **131.2 disposition (2026-09-18, `docs/architecture/127-disposition-131.md`, tkc 2.8.0 built from `386cf3d`):** reproduced — undefined symbol `_fold` at link (no glue), not bad IR; **workaround-is-canonical: the canonical form is `xs.reduce(init;&f)`, which works today**; a `fold` alias is a 2-line addition if ever wanted. **RE-PROBED 2026-09-19 (card v2 audit): `arr.fold` no longer reproduces** — it compiles, runs and returns the correct value. Whichever of the Epic 127 codegen or glue fixes resolved it, the workaround has been removed from the syntax card. Close this row after confirming with a conform case, and check whether the catalogue entries that avoided `fold` (`acc-sum`, `iter-filter-sum`) should regain it as a candidate form at the next 131.25 re-measure. |

| 131.66 | Concurrent sessions sweep each other's staged files into unrelated commits | open | P1 | **New (2026-09-19, 131.25; the fourth occurrence this session — also hit 131.38, 131.41(b), 132.0, 131.40).** Workers share one git index per repository, so a `git add` by one and a `git commit` by another lands the first worker's staged files in the second's commit — 131.25's fixture rename went into commit `9c483e6`. Nothing has been lost so far because content is verified by diff afterwards, but provenance is wrong in several commits and a future collision could commit half-finished work. Binary pinning (131.39) protected the *runs*; it does not protect the *tree*. Options: require every worker to commit via a private index (`GIT_INDEX_FILE`), or serialise commits through a lock, or have workers hand patches to the main thread. Decide one and put it in `AGENTS.md` as a standing rule. **Guidance correction 2026-09-19:** my "commit via a private index" instruction was incomplete and nearly caused real damage — a worker used `GIT_INDEX_FILE=$(mktemp)` **unseeded**, which produced a tree-wiping commit (every other file read as deleted). Caught immediately and reset, but the rule must be: `export GIT_INDEX_FILE=$(mktemp) && git read-tree HEAD && git add <your paths> && git commit`, **then verify the commit touched only the files you intended** (`git show --stat`). Put that exact sequence in `AGENTS.md`, not the shorthand. **Guidance correction 3 (2026-09-19, from 131.69) — there is a FIFTH step.** Committing through a private index leaves the **shared** `.git/index` stale: after the commit it still describes the old HEAD, so the committer's files appear there as staged deletions or reversions, and **the next agent to run a plain `git commit` would sweep them in** — which is the very failure this mitigation exists to prevent, merely displaced onto the next worker. Full rule for `AGENTS.md`: (1) `export GIT_INDEX_FILE=$(mktemp)`; (2) `git read-tree HEAD`; (3) `git add <paths>`; (4) `git commit`, then `git show --stat` to verify only the intended files landed; (5) **`git reset HEAD -- <paths>`** against the shared index, confirmed with `git diff --cached --name-only`. Verified clean in toke-corpus after the 131.69 commit. **It happened again on 2026-09-19, and this time I caused it.** My own `progress: 128.19 done` commit (`00347fc`) was made with a plain `git add docs/progress.md && git commit` against the **shared** index, which still held another agent's staged state. It committed a **wholesale revert of story 127.64's work** — 226 deletions across `src/llvm.c`, `src/types.c` and both new test files — while its message described only a progress update. The worker caught it and restored in `6f95bb5`; I verified HEAD is byte-identical to its original `1b52fcf` and the fact-table counts agree (223 YAML, 8 shell, 231 total). **Two conclusions.** First, the five-step rule applies to the **main thread too**, including routine `progress.md` commits — I wrote the rule for agents and then broke it myself within the hour. Second, `git show --stat` after committing is not optional: the damage was invisible in the commit message and would have been silent without it.|

### Epic 128 — Training strategy reset: base-model bake-off, fine-tune vs from-scratch, multi-model pipeline (2026-08-09)

**Why:** the Gate-2 fine-tuned model was **not good at writing toke** — 55.6% functional (272/489), and the 101.R1 re-audit found 1093/1748 COMPILE_FAIL under later compilers. Two compounding causes: (1) **poor training-data quality**, on which we now have significant uplift — the v0.4 corpus regen (Epic 116-C/118.3, `toke-corpus/regen/REBUILD_STATUS.md`) is delivering ~23.4k accepted records at ~98%/shard under tkc 2.8.0, plus the 1460 dual-verified library programs (Epic 126); and (2) **the base model was never assessed for toke aptitude before fine-tuning** — we fine-tuned Qwen 2.5 Coder 7B without first measuring which base model is strongest at writing toke when given a presumed verbose, high-quality prompt set that explains how to write it. This epic fixes both: a rigorous **base-model bake-off first**, then an evidence-driven decision on the training architecture. **Nothing previously decided is binding** — the "LOCKED" table in `spec/training-next-phase.md` was locked *for that (v0.3) phase only* and is explicitly reopened here; the goal is the **optimal solution built from greenfields**, including any custom/personalised components needed to get the most out of toke and achieve its goals (Epic 123 north star: a model that emits correct, token-dense toke first-try). Three strategic questions this epic must answer with data, not assumption: **(A)** which base model is strongest at toke (prompted, pre-fine-tune)? **(B)** is the fine-tune step even needed, or should we skip ahead to training from scratch (~1B, purpose-built BPE)? **(C)** does a **multi-model pipeline** — a frontier model doing the reasoning and writing the companion files (`.tkc.md`, per `spec/reasoning-channel.md`), and the toke model writing the toke source inside a compiler-diagnostic + test-execution repair loop — beat any single model? **Compute:** provision a new (or resume an existing) GPU-heavy EC2 instance for the fine-tuning runs, per the CUDA path in `toke-model/docs/hybrid-training.md` and the Epic 10.10.3 compute-budget doc; MLX on the Mac Studio remains the cheap-iteration path. **Public-repo rule:** no instance IPs/key paths in this doc — infra detail stays in the private repo docs. **Inputs:** `spec/training-next-phase.md` (research-review recommendations: GRPO/RLVR, adaptive curriculum, quality>>quantity, 3-round repair cap, pre-registered criteria), `spec/gate2-decision.md`, `toke-model/docs/hybrid-training.md` + `training-guide.md`, `spec/reasoning-channel.md`, Epic 116-D (tokenizer retrain), Epic 123/124 (north star + right-by-default). **Sequencing:** 128.1/128.2 gate everything; 128.3 (bake-off) before any fine-tune spend; 128.5–128.7 run on the EC2 instance; 128.9 is the decision that closes the epic. Gated on the Epic 129 corpus quality audit for the training-data freeze. **Scope extension 2026-09-19 (128.10–128.15), from the 2026-09-18 landscape review (`docs/about/reviews/landscape-2026-09-18.md`):** the epic now runs **parallel training lanes**, not just "bespoke tokenizer plus a model trained from the ground up" — a no-training constrained-decoding baseline that every other lane must beat, RLVR/execution-feedback training, tokenizer alternatives (superword vs bespoke vs base), a byte-level/tokenizer-free track, and continued-pretraining/adapters — all scored on one pre-registered scorecard at every stage.

### Epic 129 — Full training-asset quality audit: compiles-always, verified, compact, idiomatic (2026-08-09)

**Why:** we want **high-quality programs for training to encourage high-quality outputs** — and the Gate-2 lesson is that data quality is a first-order driver of model quality. This epic audits **every program asset that can reach training**: all v0.4 regen shards (00–11, ~23.4k records in `toke-corpus/corpus/regen_v04/`), the complete corpus (incl. any carried-forward records), the 1460 dual-verified library programs (Epic 126), `toke-test-programs`, doc/example programs, and fixtures. Two audit dimensions: **(1) Correctness** — no errors, correct current syntax, compiles under tkc 2.8.0 **every time**, and where a suitable harness + specified inputs/outputs exist, runs and verifies against expected results. **(2) Quality of construction** — code compacted to the **least code possible** while preserving performance and operational efficiency; **no deep if-nesting** (expression-`if`, early-exit, guard style); **small composable functions instead of large chunks**, so complex items are built from smaller sub-functions — which is both the idiom we want the model to learn and what makes programs easier for an LLM (and us) to troubleshoot, debug, and trace. Cross-refs: Epic 116-B (idiom standard, `--min`, rule-based judge), 118.5 (qwen idiom-judge gate), 118.7 (library ingest), 126 (library optimisation — preserve-outputs constraint), 119 (doc compile-health), 127 (open compiler bugs: the audit must never paper over a genuine compiler defect — per the project rule, each new one found becomes a story). **Output discipline:** every failure is ledgered and either repaired or regenerated and **re-verified**; the epic ends with a corpus freeze report that Epic 128 trains against.

### Epic 130 — Workspace audit & cleanup: archive legacy eras, every repo contributor-ready (2026-08-18)

**Why:** the tk workspace is ~33G across 15 git repos plus loose directories, and it carries the residue of every superseded era — v0.1–v0.3 language artifacts, Gate-1/Gate-2 fine-tune harnesses, phase1/phase2 corpus generation, dated backups, scratch dirs. With Epic 128 resetting training and Epic 129 freezing quality on the v0.4 assets, the repos should now contain **only what someone needs to contribute to, build on, and use toke** — compiler, spec, stdlib, docs, current corpus + regen harness, tokenizer, model pipeline, eval, MCP, examples, website. Everything legacy moves to the local `~/tk/archive/` (existing precedent: `docs-stale-pre-v0.4-20260703`) with a provenance manifest — **archived locally, removed from the repos, never deleted blind**. A full workspace survey (2026-08-18, agent fleet) found three problem classes. **(1) Legacy bulk:** ~12.5G of working-tree legacy reclaimable without touching git history — toke-model's April run 2.1G (the *same* adapter stored in 3 encodings) + `7b-qlora-p2` 1.5G + `.bak` training data 126M + 3 near-identical training-data copies 465M; toke-corpus `corpus/archive_phase1` + `phase2_deduplicated` 2.2G + `backups/` 200M + leetcode dump 431M; toke-tokenizer root corpus snapshots 311M; plus the 10G `~/tk/archive/` itself, dominated by an 8.6G model copy. **(2) Inverted git hygiene — the junk is tracked and the pipeline is not:** the main repo tracks its own 1.1M compiled `toke` binary (**105 revisions**, top-5 blobs in history, direct AGENTS.md §13 violation) and has 146M of un-gc'd loose objects; 149M (`toke-corpus data/corpus_default.jsonl`) and 108M (`toke-model training-data-p2/train.jsonl`) JSONLs are baked into history; `tokenizer_v03.json` 1.4M is the largest tracked blob in *both* toke-mcp and toke-website; toke-test-programs tracks 16,350 result files (151M). Meanwhile the actually-load-bearing work is untracked: toke-corpus has **135 untracked files including all 13 `pipeline/*.py`, 9 `infra/*.sh`, 10 `docs/*.md`, 66 scripts** (a fresh clone cannot run the pipeline); toke-eval has an entire uncommitted **1,014-file v0.3→v0.4 solutions migration**; toke-tokenizer's packaged `python/` lib and toke-model's `ollama/`+`docker/` deliverables sit outside git. **(3) Stale contributor surface:** toke-corpus README documents the dead phase-2 pipeline and never mentions `regen/` or v0.4 (highest-value doc fix); toke-model README sells Gate-1/p2 as current; workspace AGENTS.md still describes a monorepo that hasn't existed for months and has *no* rules for archive/public-private/scratch/generated-artifact policy; toke-benchmark declared itself dead 2026-05-18 (ARCHIVED.md) yet sits live with 409 untracked orphans; three repos have no remote at all, including the **private** 211M toke-cloud abandoned mid-refactor with a deleted `api-keys.ts` in its dirty state. **Execution model:** fleet of worker agents, **one repo per worker**, main thread owns acceptance (the 129.4/129.7 wave pattern); 130.1's rubric gates everything; per-repo stories 130.3–130.13 run in parallel after 130.2's rescue sweep; history rewrites (130.15) and deletions inside `archive/` (130.14) are owner-gated and run last, before verification (130.17) and close-out (130.18). **Hard rails (binding on every worker):** rescue-before-tidy — nothing valuable dies uncommitted; nothing referenced by open Epics 128/129 moves (`regen/`, banked `corpus/regen_v04/`, library manifests, benchmark sets); `hidden_tests/` isolation (AGENTS.md §3.5) is preserved — workers move/preserve but never read; toke-cloud and toke-console stay private, never pushed public; archive = move-with-manifest; hard-delete only for compile artifacts and byte-verified duplicates; every repo gets a `pre-cleanup-20260818` tag before its first change (cheap rollback). **This epic does not start until the owner ratifies 130.1** — prepared 2026-08-18, execution deferred.

### Epic 131 — Token-efficient-by-default toke: pattern catalogue, co-equal perf gate, corpus/library rewrite, tokenizer prep (2026-09-18)

**Why:** the custom v0.4 tokenizer (116.9) learns whatever surface the corpus shows it — so the corpus must **already** be written in the most token-efficient form before the tokenizer is trained, and that form must be **the default idiom, not a second pass**. Today the idiom is 9 prose rules (`docs/spec/idiom-v0.4.md`), 4 regex penalties (`toke-corpus/regen/idiom_judge.py`), and **no runtime-efficiency measurement at all** — the 129.4 "performance must not regress" obligation was never implemented (nothing in the pipeline times anything; `bench/results/` is empty). There is no verbose-vs-canonical pattern catalogue anywhere, no token counter in the regen pipeline (`metrics.py` records bytes only), and the verified library is badly style-divergent (129.3: idiom-below-floor **707**, depth p99 **10** vs corpus 4). **Owner decisions (2026-09-18):** (1) **runtime performance (wall, peak RSS, allocations) is a hard co-equal gate with token count** — a pattern is canonical only if best-or-tied on *both*; where they conflict the catalogue carries two forms (default + hot-path) with an explicit choice rule; (2) **the epic includes the corpus + library rewrite waves**, which **reopens the 2026-08-19 training-data freeze** (`toke-corpus/regen/AUDIT_129.md`) — a byte snapshot + git tag is taken first (131.12) so Epic 128 keeps a fallback, and a successor freeze `AUDIT_131.md` is declared at the end (131.27); (3) **tokenizer-plan Phase 0 (harness repair + baseline) and Phase 1 (corpus curation + manifest)** from `docs/architecture/tokenizer-v04-plan.md` are **absorbed here** (131.20–131.24); 116.9 keeps Phases 2–4 (train, sweep, TEMSpec gate, lock, integrate) and starts from the frozen, pattern-canonical manifest. **What "canonical" means here:** decided by measurement, not taste — a proxy byte-level BPE trained on the `--min`/string-masked corpus (decision metric; `--min` bytes tie-break; v03/Qwen/cl100k informational) **and** a micro-benchmark harness (median wall + bootstrap CI, peak RSS, malloc interposition alloc count, big-O check at N vs 4N); verdicts stay `provisional` until re-measured after the rewrite and again under the real v0.4 tokenizer (131.25). **Enforcement:** catalogue verdicts become `tkc --lint` pattern rules (131.9), the idiom judge re-based on those rules (131.10), a hard pattern-lint gate + proxy-token budget in `run_shard.py validate` (131.10), a generated "Patterns" block in the syntax card → **card v2** (131.11), and the generated normative spec + guide (131.11) — so every future generation, repair and prompt (128.2) inherits the efficient form by default. **Cross-refs:** 116.7 (idiom standard — stays normative, gains a pointer), 116.9 (tokenizer plan — Phase 0/1 absorbed), 118.3/118.4/118.5 (idiom rewrite / re-measure / CI gate — delivered or re-scoped here), 118.7-ingest → 131.18, 126.2/126.4 → 131.17, Epic 127 (open compiler bugs — disposition in 131.2, fixes stay 127.x and block card v2), 128.1/128.2/128.5 (consume card v2 + catalogue + freeze-131), 129.8 → 131.16, `docs/architecture/tokenizer-v04-plan.md`, TEMSpec (`toke-spec/docs/temspec.md`). **Execution model:** laptop-runnable stories first (131.1–131.14, 131.18–131.28); three LLM-spend waves (131.15 agent rewrite ~200–400 batches, 131.16 A-side regen 283 batches, 131.17 library ~65–80 batches; ≈550–770 batches ≈ 6–8 usage windows) launched **by hand**, automation stays OFF; no GPU anywhere. **Hard rails (binding on every worker):** agents never touch this file; every rewrite is test-locked (exact expected outputs) + differential-checked against the archived original binary + Tier-1 perf-checked, and the original is archived (`audit/replaced/131/`, `solutions-pre131/`) — never deleted; compiler bugs found become Epic 127 stories, never papered over; the diagnostic `fix` field only when deterministic; `tkc` SHA + `card_sha` + `catalogue_sha` pinned on every banked record; bank before re-prep; ≤100 batches per wave. **Execution checkpoint 2026-09-19 01:05 AEST:** 16 stories DONE in one session (131.1–131.7, 131.9, 131.10, 131.12, 131.20, 131.23, 131.24, 131.26, 131.35 + 131.11 merge, 131.18 plumbing) plus 127.18/127.19/127.22/127.23/127.29, 131.34/131.36, 127.20-glue. **The session usage limit terminated 9 workers mid-task** (127.6–127.10 wave — only 6 lines of `llvm.c` landed uncommitted, 127.8/127.6 tests written; 127.32 — 447 lines in `src/migrate.c` uncommitted, build clean, verification pending; 127.33; 131.37; 131.30 — `src/stdlib/fmt*.c` + `stdlib/fmt.tki` + `names.c`/`stdlib_deps.c` registration uncommitted; 131.13; 131.14 — `regen/pattern_autofix.py`, `diff_check.py`, `pattern_common.py` written, shakedown pending; 131.15 — `regen/pattern_prep.py`, `check_pattern.py` written; 131.22 — `scripts/curate_tokenizer_set.py` + `pre131` outputs written, one intermittent `--min` divergence unexplained). Tree state verified after the kill: `make` clean, `make conform` **211/211** with all WIP in place; every uncommitted diff + untracked file snapshotted to `~/tk/archive/wip-131-20260919/`. Resume rule: each relaunched worker inherits its predecessor's WIP from the working tree, never `git add -A`. Critical path: runtime measurement run (`--max-load 8`; CyberArk EPM pins a core permanently so loadavg 2 is unreachable — decision parked) → card v2 → 131.13 → 131.14 → LLM waves. **Scope extension 2026-09-19 (131.50–131.57), from the 2026-09-18 landscape review (`docs/about/reviews/landscape-2026-09-18.md`):** the epic gains measurement, trial and validation lanes — superword and byte-level token lanes, a byte-level durability spike, constrained-decoding artefacts and mask-cost benchmarks, reasoning-channel and terseness-vs-reliability A/Bs, a cost-per-solved-task harness and an agentic token decomposition. **The language base does not change**: no character-set, grammar, keyword or semantic change is in scope here — only how we measure, trial and validate it, and how many things each stage is benchmarked against.

An original that **passes** its own test cases keeps `identity` — byte-identical stdout, exactly as before, so a style rewrite still cannot change behaviour. An original that **fails** its tests **and** has a case expecting an err marker gets `repair`: the candidate must **pass** its test cases and every **non-error** stdout line must still match the original, with only the error line free to move. A failing baseline with **no** err expectation deliberately stays `identity`, because the repair rule would have nothing to permit and the stricter rule is the safe default. Error lines are identified **positionally from the spec** (`driver.expected_line_err_flags`), not by matching text — matching text would have let a candidate rename any line into an "error" line. `repair` is **opt-in**, so the 131.14 AUTO wave keeps plain byte-identity. Provenance records `diff_mode`, `behaviour: preserved\|repaired`, `baseline_tests` and `error_lines_changed`, so AUDIT_131 can separate the two claims rather than blurring them. **Both demonstrated records now bank** through the full pipeline — `A-ERR-0001v11` and `A-ERR-0001v37`, 13/13 gates green, 530→368 B / 92→50 tokens and 230→171 B / 17→15 tokens. **The negative test holds** against real tkc: a passing baseline still rejects a candidate that returns `$overflow` instead of `$divbyzero`. **New ceiling, measured over all 485 prepped A-ERR records:** 454 `repair_ok`, 2 `repair_blocked`, 29 `driver_blocked` — **structurally unbankable 456 → 31 of 1,651 (1.9%), wave ceiling 72.4% → 98.1%**, comfortably clear of the 95% floor. ### Epic 132 — Awareness and discoverability: one consistent, findable toke across the site and every registry (2026-09-18)

**Why:** external footprint is effectively zero; each surface (site, GitHub, PyPI, npm, Hugging Face, Ollama, VS Code) currently describes toke differently; a third party has taken "tokelang" on .com, GitHub and crates.io; the site still shows stale Gate-2 numbers (`toke-website/templates/index.tkt` L473/L552: "100% compilation Pass@1", "~8% functional"; `ecosystem.tkt` L89) — the honest number is **55.6% functional** (`docs/metrics-baseline.md`). **Owner story (2026-09-18, filed verbatim in intent):** as the maintainer of toke, I want the language named, described and marked up identically everywhere it appears, and the website updated to carry that canonical description, so that people and LLMs searching for a token-efficient language for LLM code generation find toke, understand what it is within one sentence, and do not confuse it with the slang word, the cannabis brands, the TOKE crypto tokens or tokelang.com. **Acceptance criteria (all must hold for the epic to close):** *Naming* — (1) the language is "toke" (lower case) in every heading, description and README; "Token-Optimised Language" is a descriptor only, never the name; (2) **one canonical facts block** (name, type, purpose, compiler, tokenizer, benchmark, models, source, author, spec version) lives in a single source file and is reproduced word for word on the home page, `/llms.txt`, the README of every toke repo, the Hugging Face model card, and the PyPI, npm, VS Code and Ollama descriptions; (3) "tokelang" appears once on the site — the disambiguation line — and nowhere else in new content (currently 12 site files mention it); existing URLs and package scopes unchanged; (4) loke, ooke and moke are described as toke sub-projects ("toke's web framework") or removed from the marketing surface. *Clarity* — (5) the home page opens with a one-sentence definition above the fold and a "what toke is not" section (slang word, cannabis brands, TOKE crypto tokens, Tokelau, tokelang.com); (6) the console/status page shows Gate 2 functional correctness at 55%, with the 8% history and the hardcoded-input explanation, plus the August gate result; (7) no page contradicts another on any published number (honest-metrics rule: numbers come from `docs/metrics-baseline.md`). *SEO* — (8) the article is live at `/toke-programming-language` with the drafted title tag, meta description, H1, canonical URL and Open Graph tags, scoring 90+ on the Lighthouse SEO audit; (9) schema.org markup — `SoftwareSourceCode` on the home page, `FAQPage` on the article — both passing Google's Rich Results Test; (10) `sitemap.xml`, `robots.txt` and `/llms.txt` exist (sitemap + robots already at `toke-website/sites/tokelang.dev/`; llms.txt does not) and the sitemap is submitted in Search Console; (11) every registry page links back to the site and the GitHub repo, and the site links out to every registry; (12) `karwalski/toke` has an updated description and topics (programming-language, llm, code-generation, token-efficiency, compiler) and the README's first paragraph is the canonical sentence. *Measurement* — (13) Search Console is verified, with a baseline recorded on publication day (impressions, clicks, position) for "toke programming language", "toke compiler", "toke tokenizer", "toke language"; (14) a 30/60/90-day review is scheduled covering those queries plus GitHub stars, forks, traffic and non-CI package downloads. **Out of scope:** toke.com or any domain purchase, trademark searches or filings, renaming packages or scopes, paid promotion, whitepaper changes. **Dependencies (owner-named, not yet in the tree):** the August gate write-up (no 2026-08 entry exists in `metrics-baseline.md`), the Fibonacci side-by-side, and a decision on how syntax drift was handled in toke-eval (see 130.2: 8/12 sample compile-fails are pre-existing v0.3 `=`/`==` bugs) — tracked as 132.0. **The drafted article** (title tag, meta description, H1, OG tags, four placeholders) is **not in any repo** — 132.3 starts by committing it. **Definition of done:** all 14 criteria met, changes deployed on tokelang.dev (deploy is owner-approval-gated per 116.13-H4 / 117.6), registries updated, baseline recorded, PR merged and linked here. **Estimate:** 8 points; if it doesn't fit a sprint, split along the criteria headers — site (naming + clarity) first, then registries + SEO, then measurement. **Cross-refs:** Epic 115 (Coin Gold redesign — 115.6 home/hero, 115.9 ecosystem, 115.11 voice/copy pass, 115.14 build+deploy: coordinate so copy is written once), 116.13-H4 (website v0.4 syntax pass — token-viz regeneration is separately gated on the 116.9 tokenizer; do not block on it), 119 (docs compile-health gate — every toke fence in new pages must pass `check_doc_examples.py`), 123.2 (single source of truth for status), `docs/metrics-baseline.md` (honest numbers), `feedback_no_ips_in_public` rule (no infra details in public copy). **Scope extension 2026-09-19 (132.7–132.11), from the 2026-09-18 landscape review (`docs/about/reviews/landscape-2026-09-18.md`):** the framing is repositioned from "a more token-efficient language" to "a minimal, LL(1), compiler-verified language designed for LLM code generation", with token efficiency kept as one measured, lane-qualified property. The "designed for LLMs" framing stays — it is what the supportive evidence endorses. Adds the repositioning brief (gating), whitepaper/RFC v2, a website roadmap-and-timeline page, README alignment, and an honest landscape page.

### Epic 133 — Competitive review + benchmarking: KERN / KERN-py vs toke (2026-09-18)

**Why:** a third-party project, **KERN** (Oscar Martinez, https://oscarcode9.github.io/kern-language.html — "a reversible DSL that transpiles bidirectionally between compact Kern syntax and Python, designed for token efficiency in LLM-generated code"; published 2026-03-03, updated 2026-08-01, grammar v0.4, licence/repo **not stated** on the page), publishes benchmarks **directly against toke**: "vs Toke — 60 JSON-CLI pairs — Toke 29/60 pass, 6,347 tokens vs Kern Compact 3,012 (−52.54%, cl100k_base)" and "Kern-16K vs Toke-16K on the same 60 pairs: 2,788 vs 3,906 tokens (−28.62%)". Its headline claims: −28.25% cl100k tokens vs Python over 1,682 EvalPlus/BigCodeBench programs, +4.56% beyond python-minifier 3.2.0, 541/542 Pass@1 via transpile-to-Python + execute, and a "Kern-16K" BPE (16,384 vocab) trained on **25,953** Kern Compact programs — **exactly the record count of toke's Gate-2 corpus** (`toke-model/training-data-v03`, 25,953 records), which the review must explain (coincidence, derived from our public corpus, or the same task set). We do not know which toke version, tokenizer ("Toke-16K" — we shipped 8k/32k SentencePiece and `tokenizer_v03.json`, never a 16K), syntax (v0.3 vs v0.4) or compiler produced the 29/60, nor what the 60 pairs are. The comparison is also **apples-to-oranges by design**: KERN is a Python surface-syntax compressor (the semantics, runtime and test suites are Python's), toke is a compiled language with its own runtime — which is precisely why TEMSpec (`toke-spec/docs/temspec.md`) separates same-tokenizer `token_reduction` (pass/fail) from cross-language `density_ratio` (informational). The owner wants (1) a rigorous review of the page and its benchmarks, and (2) KERN-py adopted as a standing baseline in toke-eval so every future toke number is reported next to it. **Honest-metrics rule applies:** nothing from this epic is published without the methodology; our own comparison must be reproducible by KERN's author. **Cross-refs:** `docs/about/competitive-matrix.md` + `toke-spec/docs/prior-art.md` (no KERN entry yet), TEMSpec §2.3/§6.2 (cross-language density), Epic 40 (benchmark expansion — stale), 128.1 (the v0.4 held-out set this must use), Epic 131 (canonical corpus — re-run after the rewrite), 116.9 (same-tokenizer comparison needs our locked v0.4 tokenizer), Epic 132 (publication of any resulting numbers on the site), `docs/metrics-baseline.md`. **Correction (2026-09-18, 133.1):** "Toke-16K" IS our own tokenizer — `tokenizer_v03.json` has a 16,384 vocab and ships in the PyPI wheel `toke-tokenizer==0.1.0`; and the 25,953 count is a deliberate size-match on CodeSearchNet Python functions, not our data. Their numbers reproduce to the token; the 29/60 is compiler drift on our stale April artefact in toke-eval, not a model metric.

### Epic 134 — ooke uplift to current toke, website relaunch, and a release ooke for downstream projects (2026-09-19)

**Why:** ooke is toke's web framework and the thing the public site actually runs on, so it is both the largest real-world toke program we own and the most visible proof that toke works. It has drifted. A survey on 2026-09-19 found: `ooke.toml` declares **`mintoke = "2.0.0"`** while the compiler is at **2.8.0**; `src/serve.tk` still declares **`:void` return types**, which tkc 2.8.0 warns on as a C-ism (W1020) and which the v0.4 migrator was taught to rewrite (127.32); **19 of 30 `.tk` files fail a standalone `tkc --check`** (mostly E2030 on `ooke.*` module imports, so this may be an include-path/tooling gap rather than broken source — the audit must establish which, because a file that only compiles inside one Makefile invocation cannot be linted, measured or gated); and **story 117.3, the idiom pass, has been `planned` since 2026-07-02** — meaning none of Epic 131's work reaches ooke today: not the 46-pattern catalogue, not the six `tkc --lint` pattern rules, not syntax card v2, not the token or runtime measurement harnesses. Meanwhile Epic 132 found that **~110 website `/docs/` pages cannot be rebuilt from source at all** (132.20) because `ooke build` aborts with RT005 and the served pages come from an unreproducible May-era mirror — so those pages still publish claims Epic 132 has withdrawn. Fixing ooke is therefore on the critical path for the site relaunch, not merely adjacent to it. Finally, **loke and moke are specified to build on ooke** (Epic 72 exists for exactly that), so whatever we ship has to be a real, versioned, documented release rather than a directory that happens to work. **Scope:** audit → correctness → standards and efficiency → test and benchmark → reproducible website build → relaunch (owner-gated) → a packaged ooke for downstream consumers. **Out of scope:** changing the toke language; redesigning the site's visual identity (that is Epic 115); anything that publishes to a registry or a server without owner approval. **Cross-refs:** 117.3 and 117.6 (absorbed here), Epic 113 (the pure-toke rebuild and ADR-0005), Epic 72 (ooke native bindings for loke), 131.9/131.11 (lint rules and card v2), 131.50–131.57 (the measurement lanes), 132.20/132.5/132.9 (the website blockers and the roadmap page), 132.22 (ooke/loke latency claims that are currently unsourced), 127.x (compiler fixes ooke will inherit).

Serving static assets under a versioned URL is the standard way to make a cache-bust reliable, and toke cannot do it. Strip the query string before resolving a static path. Worth noting the failure mode found on the way: a TLS spelling mismatch **SIGBUSes loudly**, which is how `S003` failed until `test_toml_glue.c`'s plain-global stand-in was corrected — a rare case of this project's defects being loud rather than silent.  **New (2026-09-20, 127.97).** The comments and the story text both say it is thread-local. **It is not.** So two concurrent tasks reporting errors clobber each other's, and the second caller reads the first's error — silently, and only under concurrency, which is the hardest kind of defect to reproduce. | 127.113 | A function body ending in a value expression without `<` evaluates it and returns 0 | done — and the row's own expectation falsified | **P0 — silent wrong answer, no diagnostic from compiler or lint** | **DONE 2026-09-22, `35bd23e`. E4071 added — and the blast-radius measurement falsified this row's own expectation, in the direction that matters.** The row said *"if the count is large, that is evidence for the decision"*. **The count is not large: 23 sites in ~8,900 toke sources, and 17 of them are prose examples rather than programs.** Live toke overwhelmingly writes `<`. **That does not weaken the hard-error call — it removes its only real cost**: the decision was framed as a reversible over-restriction if a bare tail were meant to be legal, and at 23 sites it is cheap to bear and cheap to reverse. **Two consequences worth more than the fix.** (1) **The corpus is not poisoned** — one hit, in `audit/replaced/`, already superseded. The validation pipeline's differential testing excluded these by construction, because a program returning 0 fails its own expected output, **so Gate 1 and Gate 2 data are not implicated.** (2) **The damage was in our documentation**: `docs/stdlib/file.md`, `csv.md`, `db.md` and `env.md` taught the broken idiom directly — `f=writefile():i64{ mt file.write(..){$ok:ok 0;$err:e 1} }`, documented as returning 1 on error and returning 0 always. **That is the vector by which this reached generated code**, and all 17 are repaired. **Method, because it is the reusable part:** `tkc --dump-ast` over every `.tk`, walking `FUNC_DECL → RETURN_SPEC / STMT_LIST` — **no regex anywhere** — and **the scanner was gated before it was trusted**, on a 4-function must-hit fixture and a 14-function must-not-hit fixture carrying exactly the shapes that broke the earlier grep (`io.println(str.concat("a";"b"))`, `@(1;2;3)`, `<(x*18) ^ (x/3)`): 4/4 and 0/14. **The diagnostic fires only where the silent 0 is a wrong answer** — a `void` tail call discards nothing and is untouched — and `fix` is populated only for arithmetic, a literal, a binding, a field or index read, a cast or a composite literal. It is **deliberately absent for a call** (which may be there for its side effect), for `!` propagation, and for `if`/`mt`, whose repair is `<` inside each arm: `<mt …` was **verified to be a valid repair and still not offered**, because a second valid repair exists and one wrong `fix` costs more than one missing one (§3.1, 131.78). **C021: 9 passed/7 failed → 16/0**, with a negative control proving the harness can tell a returned 6 from a dropped one, so a diagnostic that fired unconditionally would score 6/16. **It caught a real bug on its first run:** `test/standalone/test_split_append.tk:48`, where a missing `;` made `io.println(…) <0` parse as a **`<` comparison** rather than a return — **and the test passed only because the wrong answer and the right answer were both 0.** That is the same trap loke reported as "one that turned out to be ours". None of the 23 was deliberately relying on the zero.  **OWNER DECISION 2026-09-22.** **A bare tail expression is a hard error.** `<` is the return operator and a function body must use it; a value expression in tail position with no `<` is now a compile-time diagnostic, not a silent 0. Chosen over implicit tail return because it is correct if `<` is mandatory and a deliberate, reversible over-restriction if it is not — and **neither reading permits silently returning 0**. It also puts the project's stated migration tool, a compiler diagnostic, on the exact defect that 56.10.2 chose to work around at the call site four months ago. **Implementation order:** (1) measure the blast radius **using the compiler's AST, never a grep** — `;` is toke's argument separator as well as its statement separator, so a regex scanner cannot find statement boundaries; (2) add the diagnostic with a `fix` only where the repair is unambiguous, per `AGENTS.md` §3.1; (3) sweep the corpus, stdlib and docs, and expect real failures — each is a program that has been returning 0. **If the count is large, that is evidence for the decision, not against it.** **Relay to loke before they next build:** their T-2 workaround lifts a match into a typed-parameter function across **17 sites**, which is exactly this shape, so every one returns 0 for every variant unless written with an explicit `<`.  **New 2026-09-22, found while verifying loke's upstream report (Epic 137) — and it is not in that report.** **Verified in the main thread, not taken on trust:** `f=arith():i64{ 1+2+3 }` returns **0**; the same body written `<1+2+3` returns **6**; `f=tailif(x:i64):i64{ if(x>0){7}el{9} }` returns **0** instead of 7. It compiles with **no diagnostic at all** and `tkc --lint` says **nothing**. The IR shows the shape: the exit block loads the computed value and then discards it — `%t16 = load i64, i64* %t0` followed by `ret i64 0 ; implicit return`. Tag dispatch and arithmetic are both *correct*; only the return throws the answer away. **This is a regression of closed story 56.10.2**, whose own note records the diagnosis and the decision not to act on it: *"Match expression at end of function without `<` produced `ret ptr null ; implicit return`. All content items stored as NULL pointers. Fixed with `let r=...; <r` pattern. tkc codegen bug logged (implicit return from match)."* The call site was worked around, the codegen defect was logged and never fixed, and it was only ever about pointers — **it now silently returns 0 for `i64`, for `if`, for `mt` and for plain arithmetic.** **Why this is the most consequential defect found today.** loke's report describes its T-2 workaround as lifting a match into a function taking the sum as a typed parameter, across **17 sites**. That is exactly this shape, so **every one of those 17 lifted functions returns 0 for every variant unless it was written with an explicit `<`** — and loke cannot see it, because the programs compile and the linter is silent. **Relay to loke as a priority**; they must check all 17. It also means the "links" column of the report's own eight-row T-2 table was measuring link success on programs that silently return 0, so four of those rows are wrong for a reason unrelated to T-2. **The spec documents no implicit tail return either way**, so settle that first: if a bare tail expression is legal it must return its value, and if it is not it must be a hard error. Silently returning 0 is the one option that must not stand. This is the project's recurring root cause in its purest form — **the compiler substituting a default for something it never established** — and the eleventh instance of something passing while proving nothing. **Blast radius is NOT yet measured, and needs a real parse — do not trust a grep.** I attempted a static scan and threw the result away: it split statements on `;`, but **`;` is also toke's argument separator** (`io.println("a";"b")`) and appears inside `@(a;b)` literals, so every "tail" it reported was a mid-expression fragment (`18) ^ (x >> 3)`). Any scanner here must use the compiler's own AST, not a regex. **The count matters because it decides the fix:** if a bare tail expression is meant to be legal, the fix is to return its value; if `<` is mandatory, the fix is a hard error. **The spec supports neither outright.** It defines a block's value — *"Both arms are blocks whose value is the block's tail expression"* (`toke-spec-v0.4.md` §C, and `grammar.ebnf:119`) — and a function body is syntactically a `Block`, which argues for the value; but nothing states that a function body's tail is implicitly returned, and `<` exists as the return operator, which argues for the error. **Owner decision needed.** My recommendation is the **hard error** first, because it is correct under the second reading and a deliberate, reversible over-restriction under the first — and either way no program silently returns 0. That also matches this project's stated approach of using a compiler diagnostic to drive migration rather than working around at the call site, which is exactly what 56.10.2 did and why this is still here. |

Chosen over a corpus-wide `--fix` migration because that pays a large one-time cost to preserve a distinction toke does not otherwise surface, and would still have to clear the **12 frozen corpus originals** that no longer compile and re-run over the whole corpus before 131.27. **Widening makes the existing corpus correct by definition.** Order: land the widening rule → land the reverted `NODE_MAP_LIT` case at `types.c:970` (the two-line fix is preserved in the source at the reverted site) → confirm `test_127_8` and `test_127_27` pass → re-run `run_all.sh`, which fell to 378/22 when `.len` was typed globally → then 127.52's `__map__` retirement unblocks. **On the critical path to 131.27, the re-declared freeze.**  **New 2026-09-22 (127.106).** `src/types.c:970` has no `NODE_MAP_LIT` case, so the commonest way to make a map leaves the binding `TY_UNKNOWN` — and therefore **127.12's `.len`/`.keys` checker entries and the map-key type check that `NODE_INDEX_EXPR` has carried since 113.B.12 have never fired for it.** Dead code in the checker, not a missing feature. **The two-line fix was written and verified to work, then reverted deliberately**: `make diff-codegen` then rejects `test_127_8` and `test_127_27`, **both correct programs**, because `m.len` becomes `u64` and a bool-valued `m.get` becomes `bool` at call sites that declare `i64`. **So this is a u64/i64 coercion decision, not a typing bug** — and it is the blocker under **127.52** (the `__map__` retirement needs the checker to type these). The reasoning is left in the source at the reverted site. |

Three outcomes, and the middle one is the actual defect.** **Premise partly false: there is no bisect helper script anywhere in the repo**, so there was nothing to patch — the rule went into **`AGENTS.md` §7.1** instead, including the `exit 125` form, without which an unbuildable commit scores "good" and the bisect lies again. **Disproven:** the generated headers are fine — `stdlib_decls_gen.h` and `stdlib_dummyarg_gen.h` are included only by `src/llvm.c`, whose dependency the Makefile already declares explicitly. **Found and fixed — this is the mechanism:** `make clean` removed all 50 `.o` files and **not one of the 50 `.d` files**. They are gitignored, so they **survived every clean and every checkout** and were then `-include`d, describing another commit's include graph. Control: `make -n clean` named 0 `.d` before and 50 after, exactly paired with the 50 `.o`. **Root cause identified and deliberately not fixed:** make compares mtimes and **has no record of the command line an existing `.o` was built with**, so when a checkout changes `CFLAGS`, a `-D` or `SRCS`, **zero objects rebuild** — sources are byte-identical and mtimes unmoved — and the link mixes objects from two flag sets. `CFLAGS` bakes in `-DTKC_STDLIB_DIR` and `-ffile-prefix-map`, and `SRCS` changes often. **No dependency-file scheme can detect this; a flags stamp file would** → 136.62. Left unimplemented on purpose: it changes rebuild behaviour repo-wide and needs a validated full build, which this machine could not run tonight, and **shipping it unvalidated would be the exact failure mode this work is about.** Any past bisect result taken without a clean build stays unproven.  **New 2026-09-22 (127.106), and it silently corrupted a real investigation before being caught.** At commit `e11b371`, `make -j8` after checking out from another commit produced a `tkc` that compiled the probe to **exit 0 printing pointers**; `make clean && make` at the *identical* commit produced the RT003 trap. The `-MMD -MP` header dependency tracking does not cover whatever differs. **This is what made the first `git bisect run` pass return a docs-only commit as "first bad"** — a result that looks like a real answer. Add `make clean` to any bisect helper, note it in `AGENTS.md`, and treat any past bisect result obtained without a clean build as unproven. Sits alongside 136.41's "`check-canonical` cannot run from a worktree" and 131.79's shared-path hazards as a build-environment defect that produces confident wrong answers. |

So a type declaring a field called `kind` ends its own record at that field and **every field after it is lost**. **Measured, not reasoned:** with `kind` fourth of six fields, `tkc --check` accepted `.raw` and `.value` while `tkc --out` rejected both as fields that do not exist. **A front end and a back end disagreeing about whether a field exists is worse than either being wrong**, because the program type-checks and then fails to build — or, with a different field order, builds against a field the checker never validated. Same family as the struct-layout defects (127.86/89/90, 136.28/29) and the `.tki` scanner defect at `names.c:934`, which truncated a type at the first `]`: **a hand-rolled scanner standing in for a parser, failing on content that is legal in the format it is pretending to read.** **Not live today** — no `stdlib/*.tki` currently carries a decoy token; `std.xlsx` named its field `celltype` specifically to avoid this, and `src/stdlib/xlsx.h:101` records why. Scope that deliberately, because the scanner is on the compile path for every stdlib call. |

The user is shown a line number in a temporary file they have never seen and that no longer exists. **The contrast inside our own tree is the argument.** `check_doc_examples.py`'s self-test canary calls a *missing member of a known module* and gets a clean `E4027` naming the module, the member and the symbol it would have linked against. An **undefined alias** — a strictly easier case, since name resolution already knows every alias in scope — gets nothing. **Two consequences, and the second is the worse one.** A front end that says nothing and a back end that fails means the program type-checks and cannot be built, which is the same divergence as 127.134. And **before 136.26 widened the doc gate from `--check` to a full build, this whole class passed the doc gate outright** — a documented example could call through an unimported alias and be counted as proof. Emit a resolution-stage diagnostic at the call site. |
| 127.136 | A function parameter never shadows a top-level function of the same name, and the diagnostic blames the wrong thing | planned | P2 | **New 2026-09-23 (135.6).** `f=page(page:i64)` fails with **`E4031: expected 'i64', got 'func'`** — the parameter is not entering scope over the function name, so every use of `page` inside the body resolves to the function. The reverse direction gives an inverted message. **The diagnostic is the defect as much as the scoping is**: it reports a type mismatch on a correct program, and names the type of the thing it wrongly resolved rather than saying a parameter is shadowed by a function. Same family as 137.6 (cross-scope `let` shadowing) and 127.116/117, all of which were about the compiler getting scope right and then *saying* so. It cost the 135.6 worker a documentation rewrite, which is the cheap version of what it costs a consumer. Note `page` is not an exotic parameter name for a document library. |

### Epic 135 — Document and image libraries for downstream consumers (2026-09-19)

**Why.** Requested by the loke project in `~/loke/loke/docs/toke-libraries-required.md` (v1.0, 2026-09-19), written from the consumer's position so the requirements are visible before any interface is designed. It follows the pattern of the earlier ooke-bindings request, which worked: downstream states the need and the interface it expects, upstream designs and ships. **The request is unusually good and should be treated as the specification**: it states what toke already has before asking for anything, it names the constraints that rule options out, and it explicitly argues *against* the obvious answer in the one place where the obvious answer is wrong. Where it names an interface, adopt it unless there is a reason not to, and record the reason.

**The constraint that decides most of this epic: toke is a C99 project.** The link line is `-std=c99` and there are zero C++ files in the stdlib. Vendoring a C++ dependency is not an addition, it is an architectural change to what toke is, and it would impose a C++ toolchain on every toke build on every platform forever. **That is why Tesseract is rejected outright** (135.7) despite being the obvious OCR answer. There is also **no general FFI**, so every capability means a deliberate glue module plus a `.tki`, following the 43 existing `*_glue.c` modules and the `cmark`/`tomlc99` vendoring pattern in `stdlib_deps.c`.

**Nothing here blocks loke.** Its MK21 ships CSV only, states that limitation plainly, and handles extraction through a local sidecar process. These libraries let that sidecar be retired, which is the goal — the existing sidecar demonstrates the risk, since its checked-in virtualenv does not contain its own dependencies and cannot run.

**Order is by unblocked-capability per unit of cost, not by priority label:** 135.1 zip first because it is smallest and unblocks the most, then 135.2 csv, 135.3 pdf, 135.4 xlsx, 135.6 platform OCR, 135.5 image, and 135.8 as a separate project begun deliberately rather than against a deadline. Cross-refs: Epic 127 (compiler and stdlib defects), 134.11 (the ooke native-bindings surface loke also needs).

| 135.5 | `std.image` — four gaps that matter for document work | done — and two of the four "gaps" were already implemented | P3 | **DONE 2026-09-23, `b3057c9`…`002c597`. Two of the four "gaps" were not gaps — and that is the finding.** **`image_rotate()` (inverse-mapped, arbitrary-angle, bilinear) and `image_blur()` have been in `src/stdlib/image.c` since story 34.3.1.** What was missing was any way to *reach* them: no wrapper in `image_glue.c`, no entry in `stdlib/image.tki`, so `image.blur(img; 1)` did not compile. The before-run proves it verbatim — `E4027: module 'std.image' has no member 'blur'`. **This is the 136.16 / 136.44 class a third time: a finished C core behind a surface that does not expose it.** So the work split into genuinely new C (adaptive threshold, convolution, TIFF) and **pure exposure** for the other two. **Six entry points, all spellable without `_`.** **Thresholding is Sauvola, chosen with a reason rather than by default:** the cheaper Bradley/Wellner thresholds at the local mean less a percentage and **has no notion of contrast**, so over a blank margin — where the mean *is* the paper colour — roughly half the pixels fall each side and the margin fills with speckle. Sauvola's standard-deviation term collapses the bracket to `(1 − k)` where `s → 0`, so blank regions stay white. Integral images make cost independent of window size. **The test measures exactly that: 0 of 504 sampled paper pixels speckled.** **Convolution is a general odd-sized kernel rather than a second fixed filter** — `blur` and `sharpen` are each one hard-coded 3×3, and every further kernel would otherwise be new C for the same loop; `divisor = 0.0` means normalise by the kernel sum, so a zero-sum Sobel or Laplacian is left unscaled rather than divided by zero. **TIFF: ~450 lines of C99 reusing the DEFLATE inflater already there for PNG — no library vendored, per ADR-0015.** Both byte orders, the full IFD chain, compression 1/5/8/32946/32773, 1/4/8/16 bps, WhiteIsZero/BlackIsZero/RGB/Palette, Predictor 2; CCITT G3/G4, JPEG-in-TIFF, tiled, PlanarConfiguration 2 and BigTIFF are **refused by name** rather than as "decode failed". `image.decode` auto-detects TIFF, so existing callers gain it unchanged. **Multi-page cannot pass by accident:** the three fixture pages differ in width, height, channel count *and* compression, so a decoder ignoring the IFD chain would have to return a 5×4 grey plane where a 6×3 RGB one is expected — and it was **cross-checked against PIL as an independent encoder**, with raw, PackBits, LZW and Deflate each byte-exact. **C030: 1 passed/8 failed → 34/0; `test-stdlib-image` 94 → 130.** **The test design is the part to copy:** the adaptive-threshold fixture asserts its own adversarial property *first* — brightest ink 116 is lighter than darkest paper 40, **so no global threshold can pass the test for the feature the row called most valuable** — and the script tail requires `FAIL == 0 && PASS > 25`, so a run that silently did nothing fails rather than passes. The before-run also caught a real defect in the agent's own test (`$imgbuf.width` is `u32`, the helper took `i64`).  Extend the existing module, which covers more than expected. **Arbitrary-angle rotation with interpolation** — `fliph`/`flipv` exist but deskew needs real rotation. **Adaptive thresholding** — the single most valuable addition, because global thresholding fails on unevenly lit scans, which is most scans. **Convolution or a blur primitive** — for noise reduction before thresholding, and reusable well beyond OCR. **TIFF decode**, including multi-page, which is still common in financial and legal document flows and is currently unsupported. These belong here rather than in an OCR project because other consumers want them too. |

### Epic 136 — The bindings surface loke depends on does not work as documented (2026-09-19)

**Why.** Story 134.11 verified loke's bindings request against the code rather than the documentation, and compiled real consumers against each module. The request has been **archived by loke as COMPLETE, with a claim of 306 passing tests**. It is not complete. Across the 9 modules, **18 of 56 documented functions have no symbol at all, and 9 more have arity mismatches between the `.tki` interface and the actual ABI**. Two of the three P1 groups are unusable as published: webview has no glue module whatsoever and nothing links; keychain compiles but fails to link on empty framework flags. A third, secure_mem, is unimportable under its documented name because the lexer rejects the underscore. vecstore **segfaults if you call it exactly as its own interface documents**.

**The reason this is an epic and not a bug list.** Archiving the request means nobody downstream will re-check it. loke will write against the published interface, and the failure modes are the quiet kind: a missing symbol surfaces as a link error naming a mangled name, and an arity mismatch produces **silent corruption rather than a compile error**, because the compiler never validates a call against the `.tki` it was declared in. That last point is the root enabler and is filed as 136.6 — every other row in this epic is a symptom of a contract that nothing enforces. It is the same shape as 127.77, where a misspelled stdlib member escapes name resolution and surfaces as a linker failure.

**One structural finding that changes who owns this.** All 9 modules live in **toke's** stdlib, not in ooke — ooke exposes none of them. So every binding pins to a toke **commit** rather than a version (134.15), and every consumer needs an explicit stdlib include path or the compiler cannot locate the directory at all. The request was addressed to ooke; the surface is toke's.

Verified on toke `19f90f38` / ooke `b6637971` with a pinned compiler; scratch consumers only, nothing committed, and `~/loke/` was read-only throughout. Cross-refs: 134.11, 134.15, 127.77, Epic 135 (the next request from the same consumer).

Fix with `git rm --cached`, then verify with the `check-ignore --no-index` sweep above, which should return empty. **What this is *not*, so nobody re-investigates:** it is **not** a false-pass hazard for the stdlib suites. Each `test-*` recipe recompiles its binary unconditionally with an explicit `$(CC)` line, and `make -q toke` returns 1 in a fresh clone because the object files are absent — both checked. | 136.43 | Three sibling repos held armed staged reverts of the 2026-09-19 factual corrections | planned | **P0 — a bare `git commit` in any of those repos fires it** | **New 2026-09-22, found while clearing the last red gate — and found only by accident.** Sweeping every repo under `~/tk` for staged content turned up **three loaded indexes, in three different repos, each staging a revert of a correction committed on 2026-09-19**, and in every case the worktree was identical to HEAD, so `git diff` showed nothing and only `git diff --cached` revealed them. **toke-corpus** staged a revert of `8b45118` "Correct the quoted Gate 1 Pass@1 baseline to 58.8%" — the staged blob of `docs/CORPUS_REVIEW.md` contains **zero** occurrences of 58.8 where HEAD contains two, and would have restored "Gate 1 PASSED" and `63.7%` and deleted the re-opened verdict. **toke-spec** staged a revert of `53be5e0` "Correct Gate 1 Pass@1 to 58.8% across the spec docs and the RFC draft" across 8 files, 33 insertions against **150 deletions**; the RFC draft loses all 9 correction markers. **toke-console** staged the restoration of the withdrawn "87K lines of working toke" claim on a **public page**, deleting the note recording that the count does not reproduce (85,059 tracked lines). All three defused with `git restore --staged`, worktrees untouched, nothing lost; a re-sweep is clean. **Why this is P0 and not hygiene:** these were aimed at the single most consequential fact in the project, the Gate 1 verdict, which took 48 files across 7 repos to correct. They fire on the next bare `git commit` in those repos by anyone, for any reason, and the result reads as a deliberate retraction. This is the same defect as the three reverts that **did** fire on 2026-09-21 (`00347fc`, `5334d4f`, `3771868`), now shown to be **cross-repo and long-lived** rather than a same-session race. **What the existing rule does and does not cover:** `AGENTS.md` §7.4a's `git commit -m "…" -- <paths>` form does protect, because a pathspec commit takes worktree content for the named paths and ignores the index — which is why none of these fired today. It protects only the paths you name, and **not at all against a bare `git commit`**. Fix in three parts: (1) a pre-commit or CI check that fails when the index holds staged content the commit does not name; (2) a periodic sweep — `git diff --cached --name-only` across every repo — since the worktree looks clean and no existing gate reads the index; (3) settle why agents stage without committing at all, because unstaged-but-staged is never a state this project wants. **Tenth instance of a check that proves nothing:** every gate we have reads the worktree, so twelve green gates said nothing about three loaded guns. |
| 136.44 | `std.tls` is a no-op façade in front of a complete, linked, unreachable mutual-TLS implementation | done — mutual auth works end to end and fails closed | **P0 — security-relevant, and the remedy is far smaller than anyone thought** | **DONE 2026-09-22, `1f2246c` + `15731b0`. `std.tls` speaks real TLS 1.3, and mutual auth fails closed — proved on the wire by a third-party stack, not by a source claim.** Glue renamed to the interface as decided (`connecttls`/`listentls` → `connect`/`listen`); **17 wrappers, every one reaching the 910-line core** — the `.tki`'s 9 published functions plus 8 forced by the unspellable-field constraint (`mutualconfig`, `pinconfig`, `tlsconfig`, `freeconfig`, `certof`, `keyof`, `freekeypair`, `protocol`). **Mutual auth is configured only through `tls.mutualconfig(cert; key; peercert)`; no caller ever names `peer_cert_pem` or `require_mutual`**, and `certof`/`keyof` cover `TlsKeypair`'s equally unspellable fields (136.46). `tls_protocol()` added to the core (~12 lines) so *"this is TLS 1.3"* is **observable rather than asserted**. **C022: 1 passed/15 failed → 27/0.** `check-tki` **488 pass/53 quarantined → 501/48, 0 fail** — the five `tls.tki` quarantine lines deleted, not re-exempted. `conform-sh` 37/37, `check-docs` 438/438. **The refusal is witnessed positively:** an unauthenticated peer gets RFC 8446 **alert 116, `certificate_required`**, during the handshake and the toke handler never runs; the authenticated arm is the control, same script and same server, one variable. **And the first version of that test was wrong in an instructive way** — it asserted the anonymous client printed `reply=none`, which was flaky because the client takes SIGPIPE writing into a torn-down connection and its block-buffered stdout dies with it, making the observation an **empty string**. *"Relaxing to 'no reply came back' would have made it green and worthless."* An empty observation is now a failure. **A stronger claim was retracted by measurement:** `build_ssl_ctx`'s unconditional `SSL_VERIFY_PEER` clears `SSL_VERIFY_FAIL_IF_NO_PEER_CERT` whenever a peer cert is pinned, which was first written up as a fail-open — then tested with the hunk reverted, and **the door was still shut** by `accept_thread`'s post-handshake `verify_pin()`. **So this was never a live hole**; the fix moves the refusal from a bare close after a completed handshake to a protocol-level refusal during it. Defence in depth and correct layering, not a security fix — said so in the code and the commit rather than letting the stronger claim stand.  **OWNER DECISION 2026-09-22.** **Rename the C glue to match the `.tki`, and add the missing wrappers.** `tls.connect` and `tls.listen` are the published interface and the names any reader would write; `connecttls`/`listentls` are an internal spelling accident, and renaming internal C symbols costs nothing and breaks no caller. **The remedy is ~9 wrapper functions over the existing 910-line implementation, not an API redesign.** **Constraint that shapes the wrappers:** `$TlsConfig`'s `peer_cert_pem` and `require_mutual` contain underscores the 59-character profile cannot express (136.46), so **mutual-auth configuration is surfaced through a constructor, never by requiring a caller to name those fields.** **And treat this as a class, not an incident:** "glue returns 0 while the C core is complete" is now the second instance after 136.16 (`std.toon`) — sweep `mdns.c`, `mlx.c` and `infer.c`, which are reported to be the same, and any other module whose wrappers are uniformly `(void)arg; return 0;`. **Nothing may claim TLS anywhere until this lands.**  **New 2026-09-22 (Epic 137 verification), and verified in the main thread rather than taken on report.** `src/stdlib/tls.c` is **910 lines of real, working TLS 1.3**, compiled and **linked** (`stdlib_deps.c:104`, `-lssl -lcrypto`): a `TLS1_3_VERSION` floor on both min and max, **mutual TLS via `SSL_VERIFY_PEER \| SSL_VERIFY_FAIL_IF_NO_PEER_CERT` driven by `cfg.require_mutual`**, peer-certificate pinning, an **X25519MLKEM768** post-quantum hybrid key exchange, P-384/ML-DSA-65 self-signed generation and pairing codes. **None of it is reachable from toke**, and the disconnect is three-way. `tls.tki` declares `connect`, `listen`, `peercert`, `fingerprint`, `pairingcode`, `read`, `write`, `close`, `genselfsigned`. The glue defines only `tk_tls_close_w`, `tk_tls_connect**tls**_w`, `tk_tls_genselfsigned_w`, `tk_tls_listen**tls**_w`, `tk_tls_read_w`, `tk_tls_tlsconfig_w`, `tk_tls_write_w` — so **`tls.connect` mangles to `tk_tls_connect_w`, which does not exist** (the glue spells it `connecttls`), the same for `tls.listen`, and `peercert`/`fingerprint`/`pairingcode` have **no wrapper at all**. And **every wrapper that does exist is a stub**: `tk_tls_tlsconfig_w` is `(void)cert_path; (void)key_path; return 0;`, and `connecttls`, `listentls`, `read`, `write`, `close` are the same shape — while `tls_connect`, `tls_listen`, `tls_peer_cert`, `tls_fingerprint` and `tls_pairing_code` sit in the same link unit. `listentls` returns before binding a socket. **So the honest statement is not "mutual auth cannot be expressed" — it is that no TLS of any kind happens, and `std.tls` is a façade in front of a finished implementation.** This is the same shape as **136.16**, where `std.toon` was bound to stubs while the real implementations sat unused — second instance, so treat it as a class: **a module whose glue returns 0 while its C core is complete**. Sweep for others. **The remedy is roughly 9 wrapper functions and a name reconciliation, not an API redesign** — which is the actionable correction to 137.11, where loke reasonably concluded the capability was absent. `mdns.c`, `mlx.c` and `infer.c` are reportedly the same; confirm each. Do this before anything claims TLS anywhere, and note that `$TlsConfig`'s `peer_cert_pem` and `require_mutual` fields are **unspellable from toke source** (136.46), so the wrappers must not require the caller to name them. |
| 136.44a | Post-quantum certificate generation was implemented, linked and unreachable — and 136.44's own sweep could not have found it | done — wired, and the no-fallback property is what the test asserts | **P1 — security-relevant** | **DONE 2026-09-23.** `tls_gen_self_signed_alg` has been implemented and linked in `src/stdlib/tls.c:341` since **124.1 shipped ADR-0013's crypto agility (2026-07-06)** — it selects the certificate signing key, `ecdsa-p384` or **`ml-dsa-65`, post-quantum, FIPS 204** — and it had **no wrapper and no `.tki` export**, so ML-DSA certificate generation could not be reached from toke at all. **The reason it survived 136.44 is the finding, and it generalises.** That sweep compared *declared* `.tki` exports against the glue and found seventeen wrappers that named nothing or returned 0. This one **was never declared**, so there was nothing to disagree with — a capability can be invisible to a reconciliation gate precisely by being absent from both sides. The detector that does find it is different: enumerate the *public C surface* (`tls.h`) and subtract what the glue calls. Run here, it returns exactly two — `tls_gen_self_signed_alg` and `tls_conn_free_id`, the second an internal free function. **That sweep should be run across all 65 modules; it is not yet a gate.** Wired as **`tls.genselfsignedalg(commonname; validdays; keyalg)`**, resolving through the generic `tk_<mod>_<method>_w` fallback, declared in `stdlib/tls.tki` and documented in `docs/stdlib/tls.md`. **The assertion that matters is not "it produced a certificate".** It is that a caller who asked for ML-DSA-65 *got* ML-DSA-65: a classical certificate silently substituted is the worst outcome available here, because the caller asked for post-quantum precisely because it matters to them. The C core already failed closed on both paths — an unknown algorithm is an error, and an ML-DSA keygen failure is an error, neither defaults — and the wrapper does not soften it. **C022 extended from 32 to 36 assertions, 0 failed, and it is premise-first:** it first asks the linked OpenSSL whether it offers ML-DSA-65 and asserts against the answer, so **neither branch can pass vacuously** — where ML-DSA exists the certificate must parse as ML-DSA-65 *and* the `ecdsa-p384` one must parse as ECDSA, proving the two paths differ rather than one being the other; where it does not, the call must be **refused** and write no file. `rsa-1024` is refused and writes nothing in both environments. Verified on OpenSSL 3.6.4. **Two smaller corrections alongside.** `src/stdlib/tls.h` documented five toke-surface names in the underscored v0.2 spelling (`tls.gen_self_signed`, `tls.peer_cert`, `tls.pairing_code` and two more) — names no toke program can write (136.46) — now corrected. And the new wrapper **deliberately keeps the module's value-sentinel convention** (0 on failure) rather than the error box of 127.109: `tls.c` produces a real `err_msg` that **every wrapper in the file throws away**, so moving `std.tls` to the error channel is one change for the whole module, and landing a fraction of it beside a new entry point would ship that break out of band — the same reasoning `file_glue.c` records for 127.102b. **Filed as the remaining `std.tls` work.** |
| 136.45 | Toke's stdlib carries ~39 undeclared symbols whose only specification is one consumer's source tree | decided — withdraw the consumer-specific surface | **P1 — architectural** | **OWNER DECISION 2026-09-22.** **Withdraw, do not promote.** The ~39 undeclared wrappers exist because one downstream calls them: `std.string` and `std.fs` are bare aliases of `str` and `file`, so loke is using two names for each — **that is a rename on their side, not a feature on ours**. The general form of the `json.getregulations` trap, and it is much wider than one function.** Toke's own standard library contains wrappers that exist solely because a downstream project calls them, declared in no `.tki` and specified nowhere: `str_glue.c:494` — *"Aliases for type-specific str conversion names (loke uses these)"*, **24 wrappers**; `str_glue.c:551` — *"`tk_string_*` aliases (loke uses `std.string` instead of `std.str`)"*, **11 more**, under a module name that has no `.tki` at all; `file_glue.c:238` — *"fs module aliases (loke imports `std.fs`)"*, **3 more**, again no `.tki`; and `json_glue.c:545`'s `json.getregulations`, commented *"loke-specific, stub returning empty array"*. **Two go beyond aliasing into hard-coded consumer identity:** a **`loke://` URL scheme** at `src/stdlib/webview.c:415` — the only `setURLSchemeHandler` call in the file, in a module we withdrew under 136.2 — and **`~/.loke/models/` documented as a stdlib convention** at `src/stdlib/infer.h:91`. **Why this is a defect and not a convenience:** an undeclared symbol is invisible to `check-tki`, so none of this is gated; a consumer reading the `.tki` cannot find it; and **80 of loke's own live import sites resolve against surfaces with no declared members** (`std.string` 67, `std.fs` 9, `std.io` 3, `std.clipboard` 1), which means every member call on them is unchecked until link — 127.62's defect class, at scale, in a real consumer.
