Wired into `--check` and `--check-src`. **The symptom this row recorded is now cleared too:** the compiler was rebuilt and reports **`toke 3.0.0`**, so `VERSION`, `src/main.c`, `canonical.json` and the built binary all agree for the first time since the v0.4 break began. **Watched failing on the second attempt, and the first attempt is the part worth keeping.** The control was a `sed` for `#define VERSION "toke 3.0.0"`; the file has **multiple spaces**, so it matched nothing, the file was never desynced, and **I briefly read that as the gate failing to fire.** The control now asserts its own substitution applied before any conclusion is drawn. Desynced: exit 1, *"src/main.c: states '2.9.9'; VERSION says '3.0.0'"*. Restored: exit 0. **Same class as 127.131 and 127.124 — a check that reports nothing is indistinguishable from a check that found nothing, and that applies to the controls as much as to the gates.**  **New 2026-09-22 (134.15), and it is the direct explanation for that row existing at all.** `VERSION`, `src/main.c`'s `#define VERSION`, and `.github/workflows/release.yml`'s `GITHUB_REF_NAME` are **three separate sources of the same fact, with nothing in the Makefile or any gate deriving one from another.** All three must move together and nothing enforces it — **which is how `2.8.0` survived the entire v0.4 language break, across the `=`/`==` split, expression-`if`, the capability broker and every 127.x fix.** Derive `src/main.c` from `VERSION` at build time, or gate their equality; and have the release workflow assert the tag matches `VERSION` rather than trusting the tag alone. **Same root cause as the eleven other hand-maintained-list defects found today**, applied to the single fact a downstream most needs to trust. Note the symptom is live right now and recorded under 134.15: the built binary still prints `toke 2.8.0` while README and `canonical.json` say 3.0.0. |
| 136.61 | Four `test-stdlib-http*` targets omit `log.c` and `capabilities.c` and cannot link | planned | P2 | **New 2026-09-22 (136.57).** `test-stdlib-http`, `test-stdlib-http-cookies`, `test-stdlib-http-multipart` and `test-stdlib-http-form` all omit `src/stdlib/log.c` and `src/stdlib/capabilities.c`, which `http.c` needs for `tk_access_log_write`, `tk_error_log_*` and `tk_cap_check` — **so none of the four links, in either configuration.** `test-stdlib-http-leak`, written later under 127.65, **has the correct source list**, so the fix is to copy it. **Not in `make ci`** (line 242 invokes no `test-stdlib-*`), so CI is unaffected — which is also why nobody noticed. **Four more targets nobody runs: same class as 136.42, 136.51 and 136.56**, and the fourth sighting of it today. Fold into 136.56's pattern-rule work rather than fixing these four by hand, or the fifth sighting is already written. |
| 136.62 | `make` has no record of the flags an existing `.o` was built with, so a flag change rebuilds nothing | planned | **P1** | **New 2026-09-22 (127.118), and it is the root cause behind that row's symptom.** Make compares mtimes only. When a checkout changes `CFLAGS`, a `-D` or the `SRCS` list, **zero objects rebuild** — the sources are byte-identical and their mtimes have not moved — **and the link then mixes objects compiled under two different flag sets.** This is not hypothetical: `CFLAGS` bakes in `-DTKC_STDLIB_DIR` and `-ffile-prefix-map=$(CURDIR)=.`, both of which differ between a worktree and the main checkout, and `SRCS` changes often. **No dependency-file scheme can detect it** — `-MMD -MP` tracks headers, not command lines. The fix is a **flags stamp file**: hash the effective compile command into a file that every object depends on, so a flag change forces a rebuild the same way a header change does. **Deliberately not implemented tonight** — it changes rebuild behaviour repo-wide and needs a validated full build to land safely, and shipping it unvalidated would be precisely the failure mode it exists to prevent. Until then, `AGENTS.md` §7.1's `make clean` rule is the mitigation. |
| 123.10a | `security-nightly.yml` invokes four Makefile targets that do not exist | done — and the spec it would have been implemented from is itself stale | **P1** | **DONE 2026-09-22, `faa2c4a`, split by what could be made real.** **Added `sbom` and `cve-scan`** (with `.PHONY`) from Section 3 of `ci-security.md`, which specifies them completely and depends on nothing missing. **Removed the fuzz job and its 03:00 cron rather than leave it failing — because it cannot be made to pass.** Section 2 of `ci-security.md` is **itself stale**: it builds `fuzz_md.c` and `fuzz_security.c`, **neither of which exists**; it omits four harnesses that do (multipart, template, toml, ws_frame); and it points runners at `test/fuzz/corpus/<format>/` directories that do not exist, since the corpus holds `.tk` files. **Pasting it verbatim would have left the job exactly as red** — which is the trap worth recording, because the next worker would have done precisely that. The workflow's own NOTE admitted it shipped red awaiting a Makefile change that never landed. Control: resolving every `run: make <target>` with `make -n` gives 2 targets / 0 missing after, against 4 / 2 missing before, and `make -n fuzz-120-22` still exits 2 so the check is not vacuous. **Merge this into 123.10** — `test/fuzz/` has 12 harnesses and 4 rules, and the 8 orphans are exactly what `fuzz-120-22` would have built, so the job, the targets, the corpora and a corrected Section 2 belong in one piece of work.  **New 2026-09-22 (136.51's sweep), filed against 123.10 which already owns the 8 orphaned fuzz harnesses.** The workflow calls `make fuzz-120-22`, `make fuzz-120-22-run`, `make sbom` and `make cve-scan`, and **none of the four exists in the Makefile** — so the security nightly is **red by construction** and has been failing for a reason unrelated to security. Either add the targets or remove the steps; a workflow that cannot pass is one more piece of output people learn to ignore, exactly like 136.55's unclearable warning. |

### Epic 137 — Issues found by loke building 217 modules against the current toolchain (2026-09-22)

**Source.** `~/loke/loke/docs/upstream/toke-issues.md`, written by the loke project on 2026-09-20 against toke `1bc4a44` and ooke `v3.0.0-rc.1`, while migrating 217 modules from a four-month-old API to the current one and linking them for the first time. Every issue carries a complete minimal program its author actually compiled, or — where a minimal case did not reproduce — the real loke function and the emitted IR. Each also carries the workaround loke is using, so **none of this blocks them today**; what it blocks is the next person to hit it without loke's IR-reading skills.

**The finding that matters more than any single bug.** Five of the seven build-breaking issues have the same shape: **toke accepts the program and the failure appears at link time, in LLVM's words, naming no toke source file, function or line.** A user gets `Terminator found in the middle of a basic block! label %rm_err11` and has nothing to search for. Finding the cause of each of these meant reading emitted IR and bisecting by hand, and **three of the four quality sweeps loke now runs exist only to recover information the compiler already had and discarded.** That is the through-line of the epic, and 137.13 is the story for it.

**Why the silent ones are the expensive ones.** T-4, T-6, T-7, T-9 and T-12 each let a wrong program look right, and in loke each one hid working-looking code that did nothing: a privacy opt-out that was never honoured, a config file that has never been read, a script-stripping sanitiser that matched nothing, a policy engine that can never produce a violation. This is the **same pattern this project has hit eight times in its own gates** — a check that passes while proving nothing — arriving from the other side as a language that accepts a program while meaning nothing by it.

**Status discipline for this epic.** Every row below is filed from the report and **not yet reproduced at HEAD**. The report predates two days of heavy compiler work — 127.6 through 127.14, 127.27, 127.41, 127.64, 127.80, 127.83, 127.86/89/90, 127.93, 127.95, 127.97, 126.7, 136.1 — so some rows are probably already closed. A verification pass is running; rows will be corrected from its findings rather than from the report's word. **Do not start a row until its verdict lands**, except where it is already owned by an Epic 127 story.

Cross-refs: T-5 is **127.111**, T-7 is **127.62** and **127.77**, T-4 is the unfixed half of **127.90**, T-8 is **127.81** and **127.82** (both done — expected already closed), T-6 has history in **126.7** and **114.7**, T-10 and T-12 overlap **136.6** and **136.7**. Epic 135 and Epic 136 are earlier requests from the same consumer.

| ID | Story | Status | Priority | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 137.1 | `$ok(<bool>)` in a `bool!$err` function emits invalid IR, so `bool!$errtype` is unusable | done — and the mechanism is narrower than even the correction said | **P1** | **DONE 2026-09-22, `a8131a3`. The report's mechanism was wrong, and so was my correction of it.** I recorded that "the coercion must consult the operand's actual type". **The coercion chain is complete and correct — it was being told the wrong source type.** `$ok(e)` **is not a call at all**: `emit_expr` lowers a one-argument call to a non-function, non-variant name by **passing the argument straight through**, so the value carries the argument's type — while `expr_llvm_type` answered `i64` for all of them. Every coercion site downstream was honestly coercing from a type that was not the operand's. **Fixed at the oracle, not at the site** — and that is the point worth keeping: **127.27 and 127.93 each stated the rule "the two answers must not diverge" and each applied it to one site.** This is the third time, so fix the answer rather than the caller. Breadth measured: `bool` and `f64` payloads fail; `i64`, `str` and `i32` were unaffected. **C026, 32 assertions, 20 failing at baseline → 0.**  **Verified 2026-09-22 at `1cc4761`: still reproduces, but the report's mechanism is wrong and its suggested fix would not work.** The report says toke emits `inttoptr i64` on an `i1` without widening and asks for a `zext`. What actually happens: the function is *declared* `i1` (the error travels out-of-band in `@tk_current_error`), the callee already returns `i1`, and codegen emits a blind **`trunc i64 %t4 to i1`** — a coercion to the declared return type that assumes its operand is `i64`. Error: `'%t4' defined with type 'i1' but expected 'i64'`. **Adding a `zext` would not fix it; the coercion must consult the operand's actual type.** 127.27 fixed exactly this class for map literals and did not generalise — so fix it generally this time.  **T-1.** toke emits `inttoptr i64 %t` on an `i1` without widening it first, and clang rejects it: `'%t4' defined with type 'i1' but expected 'i64'`. Confirmed in loke's own `core/mcp/client.tk`, where the emitted IR reads `%t173 = call fastcc i1 @…` followed by `%t174 = inttoptr i64 %t173 to i8*`. **Three workarounds do not work** — binding the bool to a local first, using a bool literal, and branching so each arm returns `$ok(true)`/`$ok(false)` all fail identically. loke declares the function `i64!$errtype` and returns `$ok(1)`/`$ok(0)`. Suggested fix: `zext i1 … to i64` before the `inttoptr`, wherever a success value is boxed into the result representation. **Same family as 137.5** — only an i64-width success type survives the `!$err` lowering — and **127.27** was the same `i1`-versus-`i64` confusion in map literals, so check its fix for the pattern to copy. |
| 137.2 | A `mt` of 3+ arms whose subject type is not known emits duplicate basic-block labels | done as a DIAGNOSTIC, not a capability — read the scope note before relaying to loke | **P1 — loke's #2 ask** | **DONE 2026-09-22, `e6655a4` — as a diagnostic. The capability is a separate, unfiled piece of work.** The report's per-arm label counter is confirmed wrong; its secondary suggestion is implemented as **E9005**: a 3+-arm match on a subject whose sum type is not established is now a clean error naming the fix, instead of invalid IR from LLVM naming nothing. **Cannot regress a working program** — every 3+-arm match reaching that path already produced invalid IR, and **0 of 498 repo `.tk` files trip it**. **The scope note that matters for the relay: loke's 17 sites still need the annotation.** They now get a clear error telling them so rather than `Terminator found in the middle of a basic block!`, which is the whole of what changed for them. **If 3+-arm matches on unannotated subjects should actually work, that is a follow-on** — teaching `expr_struct_type` to track sum types through array elements and `i64` parameters — and the worker deliberately did not invent that story. Two shapes reproduce it: a sum value read back out of an array, and one passed through an `i64`-typed parameter. The report's eight-row table was **not** reproduced, deliberately, since 127.113 confounds it. **C027, 18 assertions, 2 failing at baseline → 0.**  **Verified 2026-09-22: reproduces, and three of the report's claims break.** All eight rows re-run: rows 1/2/3/7 link, rows 4/5/6 fail, **row 8 does not reproduce** — a 3-arm `mt` nested in another match's arm links fine. So the inferred pattern *"works when toke can see the subject's sum type"* is **false in its first half**, which is the half loke built its workaround on: **the rows that link mostly return the wrong answer** (`row2 typed-param 3arm: a=0 b=0 c=0`, want 10/20/30). That is **not** this defect — it is **127.113**, the tail-expression discard, and every T-2 program in the report is written in that shape. **And the suggested fix — "the label counter should be per arm" — is the wrong mechanism:** `src/llvm.c:5928-5938` shows the unknown-subject match is lowered by the **result-match (`$ok`/`$err`) path**, which is structurally binary and dispatches on a single `br i1` over `@tk_current_error`, not a tag switch. Unique labels would give unreachable blocks and still-wrong dispatch. **The report's own secondary suggestion is the real fix: a match on a value whose sum type is not known should be an error in its own right.**  **T-2. The single most expensive item in loke's migration: 17 sites, each found by reading IR.** The emitted IR defines `rm_err<n>` **once per arm past the first**, so the label scheme looks like it assumes one `rm_ok`/`rm_err` pair per match — right for two arms, wrong for three or more. Error: `invalid LLVM IR input: Terminator found in the middle of a basic block!`. **The report carries an eight-row table of shapes that do and do not fail**, and infers: it works when toke can see the subject's sum type at the match, and produces invalid IR when it cannot. Notably a 2-arm match always links — which is why every `$ok`/`$err` match in the codebase is fine and this stayed hidden — and an **annotated** local links where the same unannotated local fails. loke annotates the subject or lifts the match into a function taking the sum as a typed parameter. Suggested fix: the label counter should be per arm, not per match. **And separately, a match on a value whose sum type is not known is worth an error in its own right — that is the condition that makes this reachable at all**, which is this project's own recurring root cause: the compiler proceeding on something it never established. |
| 137.3 | An `i32` used as an array index is widened with `zext i1` | done — and the row's headline understates the defect | **P1** | **DONE 2026-09-22, `a484020` + `ea4ff8c`. Correct the headline: this is not `i32`, not indices, and not one site.** I told the worker the reporter's mechanism was "exactly right" and that the row was the narrow case. **The reporter's aside was right and the row's headline is wrong** — it is a default branch taken for **any non-`i64` integer**. Verified individually: `i8`, `i16`, `i32`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32` all fail, at **all four sites**, and **one of the four — `llvm.c:4879` — defaults to `ptrtoint i8*` rather than `zext i1`, so it is invisible to the `zext i1` grep that found the others.** Fixed by routing all four through `coerce_value`. **For the record, because it shaped the test:** the `i1` arm those sites carried is **unreachable from source** — the type checker rejects a bool index and a narrow map key with E4031 — which is why the first draft of C025 asserted programs the language does not accept and failed at baseline for the wrong reason. Replaced with the reachable, load-bearing guard: the `ptrtoint i8*` arm of the same `if/else`, via a str-keyed map `.get`. **C025, 33 assertions, 24 failing at baseline → 0.**  **Verified 2026-09-22: reproduces, and this is the one case where the report's mechanism is exactly right.** `%t3 = zext i1 %t2 to i64` on a value loaded as `i32`. Sites: `src/llvm.c:4800, 4833, 4900, 4944`. The reporter's own reading — that the `zext i1` is a default branch taken for any non-`i64` integer — should be tested for breadth before fixing the narrow `i32`-index case.  **T-3.** The emitted IR loads the index as `i32` and then widens it as if it were a bool: `%t190 = zext i1 %t189 to i64` on a value loaded as `i32`. clang: `'%t189' defined with type 'i32' but expected 'i1'`. loke declares index parameters `i64`; casting at the call site also works. Suggested fix: `sext i32 … to i64` for a signed index. **The reporter's own reading is the useful part: "the `zext i1` looks like a default branch being taken for any non-`i64` integer"** — which would make this the same defect as 137.1 rather than a separate one, and would mean it affects every non-i64 integer width, not just `i32` and not just indices. Establish the real breadth before fixing the narrow case. |
| 137.4 | A bare type name in expression position gets no diagnostic | done — and the blast radius is zero | **P1 — one of loke's two "silent" asks** | **DONE 2026-09-22, `cc4c240`.** `resolve_ident` now inspects the `DeclKind`: a `NODE_IDENT` resolving to `DECL_TYPE` is E4033. **Restricted to `NODE_IDENT`** so `$thing` annotations still resolve. **Blast radius measured across 3,850 toke source files, comparing per-file diagnostic-code multisets between the old and new binaries: 0 files gained any error code, 0 gained E4033.** No legitimate bare-type position regressed, and C024 pins each as a control — `as thing` casts, `$thing{…}` literals, `:thing` annotations, a local sharing a name with a type, sum-type variant constructors, module aliases — with an undeclared name still E3011. **C024: 6 passed/13 failed → 19/0.** Also corrected the documentation: `errors.md` still described E4033 as *"member access on a type name rather than a value"*, true before this and wrong after, now *"a type name used where a value is required"* naming both spellings and both stages.  **Verified 2026-09-22: reproduces, the gap is wider than reported, and the root cause is one level up from where the report points.** E4033 lives in `src/types.c:2056` inside `NODE_FIELD_EXPR`, gated on the base being a `NODE_TYPE_IDENT` — the **`$`-prefixed spelling only**. So `$thing.n` is caught, but **the bare spelling is unchecked in every value position**, field access included: `thing.n` and `take(thing)` both give only `use of undefined value '%thing'`. That is 127.90's own case in the spelling the report renders it in. **Root cause:** `src/names.c:2156-2169` inserts a type declaration's name with `DECL_TYPE` into the *same* scope as values, and `resolve_ident` (`names.c:1307`) does a plain `scope_lookup` **without inspecting the returned `DeclKind`** — its own comment says *"toke treats type names and value names in the same namespace."* Fix in `resolve_ident`: a `NODE_IDENT` resolving to a `DECL_TYPE` is E4033. **Needs a blast-radius check against legitimate bare-type positions** (`as thing` casts, struct literals) — which is why it was not applied blind. Controls behave correctly: `take(neverdeclared)` → E3011, `take($thing)` → E4031.  **T-4.** `take(thing)` where `thing` is a type and no local of that name exists produces `use of undefined value '%thing'` from clang — no E3011, no E4033, no warning. **The gap is narrow and the message already exists:** toke reports an undefined identifier correctly when it is not also a type name, and reports E4033 for a type name used with a *field access*. A bare type name as a call argument simply is not checked. **This is the unfixed half of 127.90**, which covered the field-access case and is marked done — so verify what 127.90's fix actually reaches. In loke it hid a genuinely missing parameter in `core/policy/export.tk` and three functions in `core/policy/feedback.tk` referencing a `store` declared nowhere — **and the sibling function took `store:$store` correctly, so the two sat side by side for months.** Suggested fix: extend E4033 to a bare type name in any value position. |
| 137.5 | `void!$err` lowers to LLVM `void`, so binding the result emits `alloca void` | done — closed with 127.111 | **P1** | **Closed 2026-09-22 when 127.111 landed (`98c9694`).** Verified reproducing earlier the same day, fixed hours later: the `$ok` binding took the scrutinee's declared type while the call path already synthesises an i64 filler. C018 3/13 → 13/13. loke's 17 `void!$errtype` workarounds can be reverted.  **Verified 2026-09-22: reproduces exactly (`%v = alloca void`).** 127.111's text already has the mechanism: 127.95 fixed only the *imported* spelling, and a locally declared fallible-void function goes through the callee's return type instead of the interface cache. Note four `W1020` warnings fire first, advising `void` → `i64` — **which is precisely loke's workaround, arrived at by hand.** Work under 127.111.  **T-5.** Duplicate of **127.111** ("a user-defined fallible void function cannot be compiled at all") — recorded here only so the upstream set is complete. clang: `void type only allowed for function results`, from `%t286 = alloca void`. **loke had 17 such declarations across 8 files** and worked around them by declaring `i64!$errtype` and returning `$ok(0)`. Same family as 137.1: only an i64-width success type survives the `!$err` lowering. Suggested fix: represent a `void` success as a zero-width or i64 placeholder in the result lowering, **as `$ok(void)` already implies**. Work it under 127.111; close this row when that closes. |
| 137.6 | Any `let` shadowing an enclosing `let` emits invalid IR — and the same source defect is a silent logic bug | done — all three parts, and the load-bearing half was mutation-tested | **P1 — loke's #1 ask, and the one to fix first** | **DONE 2026-09-22, `97e6d59`. Shipped as decided: shadowing stays legal, the IR is fixed, and the warning is added.** (a) `hoist_allocas()` moves every alloca to the function entry block. (b) `NODE_STMT_LIST` pops the IR alias table with the block. (c) **W3013** warns on a `let`, `let mut` or `lp` variable shadowing an enclosing binding — **same-scope shadowing, the spec's own `let x = x + 1`, does not warn**, and no `fix` is emitted because both readings are real programs. **The second half is load-bearing and was proved so rather than assumed:** a mutant with only `c->alias_count = saved_aliases;` removed, allocas still hoisted, **compiles every case cleanly and returns the wrong answer** — 99 where 1 is correct — and C023 falls to 15/35. That is the silent-wrong-answer mode, caught at all four `-O` levels. **Prerequisite closed first, as instructed:** `cx->bind_count` is now popped with `if`/`lp`/arena scopes, so **W5001 stops naming the outer binding** as "bound in a nested block (depth 1)". **126.7 and 114.7 verified live and untouched** — `let x=5; let x=mut.10; x=x+1` → 11 with no E4070, a genuine immutable assignment still E4070, and 126.7's type-changing shadow still clean. **C023: 9 passed/26 failed → 35/0.** **Blast radius: 16 W3013 across 3,850 files (0.26%), none in stdlib, test, examples or ooke** — and **one of the sixteen is a real bug of loke's exact class**, `MSG-001`, where `let paddedpt=…` inside an `if` leaves the outer binding read afterwards. Eleven of the rest are `lp(let i=0;…)` shadowing a function-level `i`: benign, genuinely ambiguous, and exactly what the row asked to warn about.  **OWNER DECISION 2026-09-22.** **Fix the IR and add the warning; shadowing stays legal.** The recorded recommendation was "take the alloca-hoisting half; reject the reject-shadowing half", and that is **half right** — it conflates two separable things. Story 75.1.7 decided shadowing is **legal**; it did not decide it must be **silent**. So: (a) hoist every `alloca` to the function entry block, which fixes the invalid IR; (b) keep 75.1.7 Option A and the spec's published `let x = x + 1`; (c) **add a warning** — *"this `let` shadows a binding in an enclosing scope; did you mean an assignment to a `mut`?"* — which contradicts nothing and is what loke says *"would have saved most of the effort in this migration"*. The evidence for (c) is 52 shadowed bindings across 18 files, including a privacy opt-out never honoured and four job-queue transitions that were infinite loops, **all of which compiled**. **Two prerequisites:** check what 126.7 and 114.7 already closed before rebuilding, and **fix the misattributed `W5001` first** — it fires on the read of the *outer* binding claiming depth 1, and does not fire at all on the loop-body case, so a second shadowing warning beside it would compound the confusion.  **Verified 2026-09-22: reproduces as literally written, but do not implement the fix as suggested.** Right that *cross-scope* shadowing breaks, and confirmed it fails whether or not the value escapes. **Wrong that "toke has no lexical shadowing at all":** same-scope shadowing works and returns the right answer — the spec's own example `let p=x; let p=p+1;` yields 2. **And the suggested "reject or warn on a shadowing `let`" contradicts a decision this project already took:** story **75.1.7** chose *"Option A. Allow same-scope and cross-scope shadowing"*, and `docs/spec/toke-spec-v0.3.md:877` publishes `let x = x + 1;` as legal. **Take the alloca-hoisting half; reject the reject-shadowing half.** One real behaviour change since `1bc4a44`: **the silent half is gone** — loke's `privacy.tk:shouldstore` shape is now a build break rather than a wrong answer, so that class of bug can no longer ship. Separately, the new `W5001` that fires on this reproducer is **misattributed**: it fires on the read of the *outer* binding at function-body level claiming it was "bound in a nested block (depth 1)", and it does not fire at all on the loop-body case. That is its own small defect.  **T-6.** toke emits the `alloca` inside the branch and the load after it: `Instruction does not dominate all uses!`. This fails **whether or not the inner binding's value escapes the branch**, so in practice toke has no lexical shadowing at all — every occurrence is a build break. **The reason loke ranks this first is the second half.** Shadowing is also how an ordinary mistake looks: `let x=…` inside an `if` does not assign to an outer `x`, so code that reads like an assignment silently declares a second binding. loke found **52 shadowed bindings across 18 files**, including a privacy opt-out that was never honoured (real code from `core/memory/privacy.tk:shouldstore` — a user's opt-out topics were silently ignored), four job-queue state transitions that were infinite loops (`let i=i+1` never advanced the counter), a model registry that could never find a model, an always-empty Ollama model list, and a shorthand expander that returned its input unchanged. **All of them compiled.** So one fix catches two classes of bug, and the reporter says even a bare warning — *"this `let` shadows a binding in an enclosing scope; did you mean an assignment to a `mut`?"* — would have saved most of the migration effort. Suggested fix: hoist every `alloca` to the function entry block; independently, reject or warn on a shadowing `let`. **History to check first: 126.7** fixed a shadowed `let` *with a new type*, and **114.7** records a `mut`-shadow false E4070 as partially fixed — so establish what is already closed before rebuilding it. |

| 137.9 | The regex engine ignores unsupported syntax instead of rejecting it | decided — reject unsupported regex syntax at compile time | **P1** | **OWNER DECISION 2026-09-22.** **Reject unsupported syntax at compile time; stop the silent anchoring.** `\s`, `\S`, `*?`, `(?i)` and a malformed `[` all return *no match* rather than raising, because on `regcomp` failure `result` stays 0 — so **an invalid pattern is indistinguishable from no match**. That is how loke's script-stripping sanitiser passed review for months while matching nothing, on a privacy control. POSIX `REG_EXTENDED` genuinely lacks these, so the engine is behaving as designed by story 78.4.3 — **the defect is the silence, not the limitation.** Also: `tk_str_matches_w` silently wraps every pattern as `^(pattern)$`, which is a second source of silent non-matches and must stop. And give `test/standalone/test_regex.tk` its name back — it currently asserts only `startswith`/`contains`/`endswith` and tests no regex behaviour at all.  **Verified 2026-09-22: the claim holds completely, by design and by measurement — but there is no regex module.** Neither `std.regex` nor `std.re` exists; both are rejected by the 127.42 module gate, and the `tk_regex_*_w` wrappers in `src/stdlib/tk_web_glue.c:1469+` are **unreachable from user code**. The reachable surface is `str.matches`/`str.replacere`. **Mechanism:** `if (regcomp(&re, anchored, REG_EXTENDED \| REG_NOSUB) == 0) { result = … }` — **on compile failure `result` stays 0**, so an invalid pattern is indistinguishable from no match. **Design:** story 78.4.3 specifies POSIX `regex.h` with `REG_EXTENDED`, which genuinely has no `\s`, `\S`, `*?` or `(?i)`. Measured: baseline `[0-9]+` vs `123` = 1; `\s`, `\S`, `<.*?>`, `(?i)ABC` and a malformed `[` all = 0. **Two things the report missed.** `tk_str_matches_w` silently wraps the pattern as `^(pattern)$`, so loke's `str.match(code;"[a-zA-Z0-9]{32,}")` at `src/cli/code_preprocess.tk:101` demands the *whole* string be 32+ alphanumerics — almost certainly not the intent, and a second silent no-match source. And **`test/standalone/test_regex.tk`, the file named for this, tests no regex behaviour at all** — it asserts only `startswith`/`contains`/`endswith`, exactly as story 79.2.5 lists. Reject unsupported syntax at compile time, distinguish compile failure from no match, stop silently anchoring, and give the test file its name back.  **T-9.** `\s`, `\S`, non-greedy `*?` and the inline flag `(?i)` all return **no match** rather than raising, so a pattern using them compiles, runs, and quietly does nothing. **This is how loke's `privacy/content.tk` script-stripping sanitiser passed review for months: it was a privacy control that matched nothing.** Either support them or reject them at compile time — the reporter's judgement is that **silence is the worst of the three**, and this project's own experience agrees: a check that passes while proving nothing has been found eight times in our gates this session. Decide which syntax the engine supports, then make everything outside that set a diagnostic rather than a non-match. |

| 137.11 | Four stdlib modules are stubs that return plausible values, and nothing says so at the call site | corrected — three of the four are the class; `infer` is not | **P1** | **Premise corrected 2026-09-22 by measurement (136.44's sweep), on the one module it matters most for.** **`infer` is NOT the same class as `tls`.** `infer.c` is almost entirely inside `#ifdef TK_HAVE_LLAMACPP` arms, and **`TK_HAVE_LLAMACPP` is never defined anywhere in the build** — not in the Makefile, not in `stdlib_deps.c`, not in any header (the Makefile defines `TK_HAVE_OPENSSL`, never this). Measured: **164 of 397 lines compile; 214 are skipped.** So there is no working implementation sitting unused — **the core is itself a compile-time stub, and `infer` is a missing backend, not a façade.** Wiring its glue up would convert `"[infer: not available]"` — the *successful-looking* sentinel that reads as "no entities found" in loke's privacy detector — into an honest error, which is worth doing, but **it will not make inference work.** **`mdns` and `mlx` are the class**, and `mdns` is the striking one: `mdns.c` is 788 lines of **full Bonjour** on macOS (`dns_sd.h`, `DNSServiceRegister`, `DNSServiceBrowse`, `mdns_is_available()` returning 1), with real avahi and Win32 branches, and **no link flag needed** since `dns_sd` is in libSystem — 6 `.tki` exports, 5 wrappers, **0 reaching the core**. Wiring it up should simply work on this platform. `mlx` is real but is an HTTP bridge client to an external sidecar, so wiring it up converts a silent 0 into an honest *"bridge connection failed"* — smaller payoff, still worth it. Note its glue's `isavailable` returns 0 in **both** arms of its own `#if defined(__APPLE__) && defined(__arm64__)`.  **Verified 2026-09-22: every value confirmed, and loke's retraction is correct.** All four modules compile, link and run: `tlsconfig=0`, `infer.generate=[infer: not available]`, `mlx.isavailable=0`, `mdns.browse.len=0`. The underscore identifiers block nothing, because resolution mangles `alias.fn` → `tk_<mod>_<fn>_w` and never consults the `.tki` for these — **so the 209/217 ceiling was wrong and 217/217 is right.** The four glue files read exactly as quoted, including mdns's *"no handle (not available)"* comment and mlx's `#if defined(__APPLE__) && defined(__arm64__)` returning 0 anyway. **The mutual-auth claim is confirmed structurally:** `tls.tki`'s `TlsConfig` still carries `peer_cert_pem` and `require_mutual` while `tk_tls_tlsconfig_w(cert_path, key_path)` takes two arguments, so those fields have nowhere to go and mutual auth is genuinely inexpressible.  **T-11, and it contains a retraction of loke's own earlier claim.** `std.tls`, `std.mdns`, `std.infer` and `std.mlx` are present, callable, type-checked, and every function in them is a stub: `tlsconfig`/`connecttls`/`listentls`/`genselfsigned` discard their arguments and return 0 — **there is no TLS**; `mdns.advertise` returns 0 and `browse` an empty array; `infer.load` returns 0 and `generate` returns the literal string `"[infer: not available]"`; `mlx.isavailable` returns 0 unconditionally, **including on Apple Silicon**. **A stub returning a plausible value is worse than one that fails:** `infer.generate`'s sentinel arrives as a *successful* result, and in loke that path is a privacy detector where it would have read as "no entities found" — a fail-open. **Separately, `std.tls`'s signature change is not merely an arity change:** `tlsconfig` now takes `(cert, key)`, and the peer certificate and verify-peer flag — the mutual-authentication half — have nowhere to go, so "TLS 1.3 mutual auth" cannot be *expressed* through this API. loke has reopened four of its own stories on that basis. **The retraction:** loke previously told this project these four modules were **unreachable** because their `.tki` files declare underscore identifiers that toke rejects, and concluded a ceiling of 209 of 217 modules. It now says that was wrong — the compiler resolves them from its builtin table regardless of the `.tki` — and **the real figure is 217 of 217**. **This retraction does *not* touch 136.8** — that story is about `std.shell`, `std.assert` and `std.arr`, three different modules the report never mentions; I briefly recorded otherwise and it was wrong. What the retraction does give 136.8 is a lead: loke's build figure is now **217 of 217 modules**, so if every loke module builds today, either it no longer imports those three or something satisfies them — check that before assuming the story is live. Suggested fix: make stub status visible — a `capability`/`available()` predicate per module, a compile-time warning on calling a stub, or a distinguishable error rather than `0` and a sentinel string — and document it in the `.md` beside each `.tki`. **Remedy corrected 2026-09-22 — see 136.44, and it changes the size of this job by an order of magnitude.** loke reasonably concluded the capability is absent. It is not: `src/stdlib/tls.c` is **910 lines of complete, linked TLS 1.3** with mutual auth, peer-cert pinning and an X25519MLKEM768 post-quantum exchange, and the stubs are a façade in front of it. So the fix is **~9 wrapper functions and a name reconciliation, not an API redesign**. **The statement that should lead is not "mutual auth cannot be expressed" but "no TLS of any kind happens."** Also: loke's *reasoning* about the signature is wrong even though its conclusion was fair — `tls.tlsconfig` appears in no `.tki`, `.md` or spec (it is glue-only), `tls.tki` has two commits ever and **no arity ever changed**, and the mutual-auth inputs were never parameters — they are `$TlsConfig` **fields**, `peer_cert_pem` and `require_mutual`, still declared and **unspellable from toke source** (136.46). Mutual auth is blocked by three walls, none of them the one loke named. **WIDENED 2026-09-23 (135.13), and the class is bigger than "the glue returns 0".** Re-measured while bringing the module pages under the doc gate: **four exports have no `_w` symbol at all** — `mlx.unload`, `mlx.embed`, `mdns.isavailable`, `mdns.resolve` — so a documented call does not return a plausible value, it **fails at link with `E9003`**. That is a *better* failure than a silent 0 and it is still a defect, because the `.tki` publishes the export. **Worse: `mdns.browse` has lost its callback parameter in the implementation** — `.tki` `(str; fn)`, glue `(i64)` — so there is no discovery path even in principle, which is a stronger statement than "the wrapper returns 0". **`mdns.advertise` `.tki` 1 against glue 3**, and `mdns.servicerecord` links and returns 0, so the constructor constructs nothing. On `mlx`: `mlx.generate` drops `maxtokens` (`.tki` 3, glue 2) and returns the literal `"[mlx: not available]"`, and **`mlx.isavailable` returns a hard-coded 0 on every platform including Apple Silicon** while the sysctl-plus-bridge-health probe in `mlx.c` is never called. **So the remedy splits three ways — wrappers that exist and return 0, wrappers that do not exist, and wrappers whose signature has diverged from the interface — and only the first is what 136.44's sweep was shaped to find.** Sizes confirm the shape: `mlx.c` 647 lines against a 34-line glue, `mdns.c` 788 against 46. Restoration is glue only in both cases. **One more, 2026-09-23 (135.6): `mlx.isavailable` hard-returns 0 in BOTH `#if` arms while the real `mlx_is_available()` probe sits in the same file, unused.** So it is not a platform guard that happens to be false here — it is false everywhere by construction, including where the capability exists. It is also one of `check-glue-core`'s three tracked stubs, so the gate knows the file is suspect and still cannot see this. |

| 137.14 | A discarded comparison is not warned about, and `<` being both return and less-than makes it look like a return | filed — unverified at HEAD | P2 | **The report's "one that turned out to be ours" — filed anyway, because the diagnostic is ours.** `<` is both the return operator and less-than, so a call followed by `<$ok(1)` with no semicolon parses as **one comparison expression** and the function returns the comparison rather than `$ok(1)`. toke is behaving as specified, and the reporter says so plainly. But it is only *reported* when the left operand is a void call, and then it arrives as `void type only allowed for function results` from clang — a message about nothing the user wrote. **A warning on a discarded comparison would catch it, and the `discarded-value-result` rule already covers the neighbouring case** (see 127.3, in progress, and 127.37). Extend that rule rather than adding a new one. Cheap, and it closes a trap created by the 59-char set's operator reuse — worth knowing about when weighing future operator choices. |
